Second, a Unified Leaderboard (ULB) that reduces heterogeneous outcomes to pairwise evidence and fits a game-balanced Bradley-Terry model by minorization-maximization with bootstrap intervals, so that high-throughput games cannot dominate the aggregate ranking. Third, a game skill-profile methodology that scores each game along diverse skill dimensions, making the capability coverage of the suite explicit and turning game selection into a design decision rather than an artifact of availability. In this paper, we specify the research design and outcome reduction of the current implementation and evaluate the framework on a ten-game suite spanning perfect-information board games, imperfect-information games, and social/language settings, reporting LLM capability profiles, evaluation-cost savings across model-refresh cycles, and an empirical Pareto frontier relating model performance to inference cost. As deployed, the scheduler saved 61.7% of episodes; it counted each episode in the two team games as four records, overstating their savings, and the other eight games save 61.9%.

title: Vetoes and missed agreements in language-model bargaining
summary: A language model played three representatives, each instructed to get the best payoff for its own group. One representative requested a plan, another chose the sole offer, and all three voted. If anyone voted no, each group received its fallback payoff. In 60 games with Qwen3-Next-80B, the representative at risk of a loss always requested a plan that would leave everyone better off. In each game, two copies of the proposer saw the same payoffs, peer request and reminder that the offer needed three yes votes. Showing the proposer how many groups gained under each plan raised mutually beneficial agreements from 6/60 to 31/60 (paired increase 41.7 percentage points, conservative 95% interval 18.8 to 58.5). Two of the four plans benefited everyone, so picking uniformly would put a mutual gain on the ballot half the time on average. In an earlier study, GPT-4.1 played 12 conflict games under two message conditions. Majority rule passed 15 of 24 offers, all at one group's expense. Unanimity passed two, both mutual gains. In the Qwen games, voters never saw the counts. They approved all 37 offers that helped everyone. On all 83 offers that would have cost one group points, its representative voted no.

title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
summary: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

title: CausalNTP: A World-Model Recipe for Causal Next-Token Prediction under Noisy Training-data
summary: This paper shows that transformer networks trained with next-token prediction (NTP) and gradient descent do not learn to make predictions using only causally-relevant tokens in the left context, irrespective of the causal ordering of tokens during training, and identifies the learning deficiencies responsible. We introduce a causal world-model setup, for which, we characterize the Bayes-optimal predictor under the causal view of the data. We then prove that, a function that distills its predictions to non-causal views of data, when realized under Occam's Razor, recovers the true causal predictor. Based on this analysis we propose CausalNTP, a practical training algorithm that approximates this theoretical recipe and trains transformers to depend only the causally relevant tokens in left-context. Empirically in the world-model setup, CausalNTP achieves out-of-distribution generalization that vanilla NTP cannot due to its theoretical limits, regardless of data and model scale. We show similar gains and behavior in the natural language question-answering setting as a proof-of-concept.

title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
summary: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.

title: The Effect of Security-Focused Prompts on Reported Findings: A Controlled Experiment on 400 AI-Generated Web Applications
summary: Agentic coding tools turn a specification into a running web application, so their defaults for authentication, sessions, input validation, and dependencies become its security posture. This study asks whether appending a fixed block of OWASP-aligned security requirements to the prompt changes what such tools produce, by how much, and with what side effects. Each of 100 frozen specifications was realized four times: two agentic tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI) crossed with two prompts sharing a byte-identical functional core, without (A) and with (B) the security block. A fixed static and dynamic pipeline scanned the 400 applications, yielding 6,721 triaged findings, analyzed with count and logistic mixed models and with a dependency diff. The block cut findings per application by a third (incidence-rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.60-0.71), equally through both tools, and roughly doubled the declared dependency surface, so variant-B applications carried more high-severity dependency advisories. Adjusted for that surface the advisory rate did not rise (flat per application, 18% lower in aggregate), while high-severity findings in first-party source fell by nearly half. Security-focused prompting is therefore an inexpensive and portable improvement, but it enlarges the dependency surface that has to be audited against it, an effect of library selection rather than of the security requirements themselves.

title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
comment: 29 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
comment: 29 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. title: Diversity over Scale: Recursive Self-Improvement with Ensembles of Small Open-Weight Models
summary: The advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents across various tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) loops, in which a language model repeatedly rewrites a program and builds on its previous version, now perform well in machine-learning tasks, but they rely on frontier models and hundreds of calls per run. Small open-weight models are far cheaper, yet when used alone, their programs often crash and their improvements stall. We propose DiVE (diverse models evolve), an ensemble method for RSI that aims to improve creativity and diversity of generated solutions. DiVE uses three components: a shared memory, a failure log, and best-idea-wins rounds. This allows models to write candidate solutions from the same context and retain the best idea at each iteration. On 22 MLE-bench Lite competitions, an ensemble of five 8-12B open-weight models has 25.4% less test error than its average member and 16.7% less than Llama 3.3 70B, and comes within 7.1% of Qwen 3.5 122B-A10B at 75% of its cost. Diversity among small models can thus stand in for part of the scale that RSI relies on.

title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

title: Cross-Site Transformers Are Robust Heart Rate Estimators
summary: Single-site heart-rate estimation from photoplethysmography (PPG) degrades sharply under real-world motion. Multi-site PPG provides a natural solution, but existing models fuse sites as generic sensor channels rather than exploiting their hemodynamic structure: each heartbeat propagates along the arterial tree, appearing across body sites as delayed and transformed copies of the same cardiac event. We propose the Cross-Site Transformer, which introduces a hemodynamically informed inductive bias by restricting multi-sensor fusion to cross-attention between PPG sites. On WildPPG, the largest in-the-wild benchmark available, our model establishes a new single-model state of the art, reducing error by 21% over the previous best and 35% over the best prior transformer. The same cross-site restriction makes the trained network directly auditable. Because each cross-attention head lies on one directed pathway between sites, causal resample ablation can isolate and test each direction of information flow. Ablating the chest-to-wrist pathway doubles error, whereas the reverse costs far less. Encoding hemodynamic structure into attention routing thus improves real-world sensing robustness and enables rigorous auditing of multi-sensor fusion.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Runbook Improvement with Agentic Support Automation
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted manuscript of the paper published in the proceedings of the 2025 IEEE 7th International Conference on Cognitive Machine Intelligence (CogMI)
summary: Operational support is an important component of production software services. Support requests are often emergent and can come in many forms such as customer escalations or unplanned service interruption. Engineers across organizations have been successful in implementing automation to help streamline support processes but many solutions remain in the hands of human operators. A successful strategy to improve operator response times is to maintain up-to-date runbooks which are documents enumerating triage steps and remediation procedures in the face of identified incidents. This paper is an investigation into an operational system which incorporates Agentic AI into a runbook based incident resolution pattern. The bot uses information in the runbook corpus along with some system-specific tooling to guide the manual operator through the mitigation process then evaluate the outcome and suggest edits to the runbook where it found gaps and in its ability to triage the situation. By using the runbook as a medium to bridge humans and automation, the process maintains explainability and can be decoupled from the agent system. This paper demonstrates a collaboration between human operators and Agentic AI with results from an 17 week study involving 232 production incidents. We conclude with lessons on integrating LLMs into DevOps workflows, related work in AI-assisted operations, and guidance for reproducibility.

title: EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform
summary: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification
summary:
Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $Θ(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244).
  Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $Ω(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.

title: ESM-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Whether AI Agents Understand Earth System Model Physics and Code
summary: AI coding agents that modify Earth System Model (ESM) code must preserve both software interfaces and the physical assumptions encoded in them. We introduce ESM-Bench, a benchmark of 60 developer-commit tasks from 6 repositories: Noah-MP, CLM5, SUMMA, ParFlow, MOM6, and VIC. The v5 corpus contains 17 physics-based bug fixes, 16 process-representation modifications, 13 parameterization-scheme selections, and 14 parameter-optimization tasks. Each task includes a scientific objective, parent-commit source files, a reference diff, and three stored prompt variants. An artifact audit confirms that all 60 reference diffs apply to their supplied starting files. We define an eight-item patch-review rubric and audit five archived patch fixtures against the implemented local checkers. None of the five fixture diffs applies to its supplied starting files, yet three text-pattern checkers return a pass. A ParFlow expression replay disagrees with the reference slopes, and a MOM6 pattern check detects an omitted update. Inspection also identifies a retained VIC reference assignment that overwrites the intended vegetation-specific albedo. These findings expose limits of reference patches and local proxies as correctness evidence. The release provides a reproducible corpus and diagnostic tools; complete expert validation, comparative agent performance, and full-model execution remain unmeasured on v5.

title: WingBench: Benchmarking How AI Agents Search for Better Designs
summary: Design search often uses cheap learned predictions to choose which candidates deserve expensive tests, but these tests can fail, especially on the unusual designs that optimization favors. We introduce WingBench, a multifidelity benchmark in which optimizers and AI agents design transonic wings with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) inside the search. They can query a learned aerodynamic surrogate and spend a fixed budget of sequential CFD evaluations, each returning a score or a failure type. WingBench grades the design each method recommends, reporting separately whether it receives a valid score and how good that score is. Using WingBench, we contribute a study of five baseline optimizers and a comparison of three AI agent methods, which produced 6,629 CFD evaluation records. Feedback helps baseline optimizers deliver valid designs when it changes their later proposals, but the differential-evolution variant does so with lower aerodynamic quality. An open-ended research agent finds designs of similar quality to the strongest baselines over 32 CFD queries, with different prior information and unmatched total computation. In early search, our reflection and planning implementations do not consistently improve on it. We release the data, code, agent prompts, and analysis scripts for reproducibility.

title: Walks2Maps: Learning Indoor Geometry from Crowdsourced Wi-Fi RTT and Motion Trajectories
comment: This paper is accepted to NeurIPS 2026 PhysWorldAI Workshop
summary: Everyday smartphone walks offer a scalable source of indoor geometry, but their motion traces drift and their radio measurements are distorted by multipath. We present Walks2Maps, a physics-guided framework that reconstructs a shared metric map from Wi-Fi round-trip-time (RTT) and motion observations, without a floor plan, surveyed access-point (AP) coordinates, or position labels. Walks2Maps jointly estimates pedestrian trajectories, AP locations, and per-trajectory stride scales, then recovers the pathway layout from the reconstructed paths. Shared AP observations connect walks recorded in different local frames, while metric ranges constrain their relative geometry and scale. An asymmetric range loss accommodates multipath-induced excess delay. On 22 phone trajectories collected along 11 routes on an office floor with 30 APs, Walks2Maps achieves median AP and trajectory errors of 0.87 m and 0.89 m, respectively, and a walked-area F1 score of 0.985. Ablations show that radio similarity can recognize places while still producing a distorted map; retaining the metric information in RTT resolves this ambiguity. Asymmetric modeling further reduces AP error by 54% relative to a symmetric loss. These results demonstrate how radio and motion measurements can jointly reveal indoor geometry without a dedicated mapping survey. We will release the dataset and toolkit.

title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
summary: We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. For each library we measure inline claims in proofs, proof length, how often each declaration is used, and design choices such as instances and private declarations, and we read each against the variation among Mathlib's own areas. The AI-generated libraries have more inline claims per theorem, longer proofs, fewer instances, and more private declarations than the human-written ones. We release the code for the analysis as a package, lean-census, at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census.

title: X-AQA: Unifying Action Quality Assessment with Multimodal Large Language Models and Multi-Domain Learning
summary: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We construct X-AQA-40K, a training corpus comprising 40,163 samples from 22 data sources across four domains: competitive sports, fitness exercises, rehabilitation, and general skills. We convert heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format, incorporating dataset-specific annotation guidelines and official scoring rules when available. Using this corpus, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to develop a single MLLM capable of handling diverse AQA tasks. We further establish X-AQA-Bench, which evaluates both in-distribution (ID) performance on datasets represented during training and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on four held-out datasets. The resulting model outperforms all evaluated open-source MLLMs on X-AQA-Bench and achieves competitive performance relative to proprietary MLLMs. Ablation studies further demonstrate that multi-domain joint training and explicitly providing assessment criteria in prompts both improve OOD generalization. X-AQA establishes a unified foundation for advancing general-purpose AQA across diverse real-world domains. Data and models are released at \hyperlink{https://huggingface.co/collections/Kelly0510/x-aqa}{here}.

title: PFN-Syn: Generating Synthetic Tabular Data with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. VLDB 2026 Workshop: Tabular Data Analysis (TaDA). Code: https://github.com/brains-group/table-agent-toolkit
summary: Synthetic tabular data can help enable data sharing and model development in privacy-sensitive domains, but existing generators often require dataset-specific training and substantial computation. We introduce PFN-Syn, a training-free framework for synthetic tabular data generation based on prior-data fitted networks. We evaluate PFN-Syn against training-based generators on eight binary classification datasets. PFN-Syn achieves the highest average downstream utility among evaluated synthetic generators, with higher generation throughput than training-based baselines, while maintaining competitive distributional similarity and distance-to-closest-record privacy behavior. Our results suggest that tabular foundation models can serve as useful building blocks for practical synthetic tabular data generation.

title: From atomic events to material degradation across metre and year scales
summary: Material degradation emerges from microscopic events whose consequences accumulate over years, yet mechanism-resolved simulations remain confined below engineering timescales. The challenge is not just the sheer number of events: atomistic evolution is dominated by recurrent local motion, with only a tiny fraction driving lasting structural change. This distinction is not encoded in an instantaneous atomic configuration. Locally indistinguishable states can exhibit different event competition, escape times, and long-horizon outcomes, revealing missing kinetic context as a critical information bottleneck. This context spans space and time: the future consequence of a local transition depends on its surrounding defect environment and the kinetic history leading to its current state. To solve this, AtomWorld reconstructs a predictive kinetic state from multiscale structural observations and trajectory history, distinguishing transient fluctuations from microscopic pathways that drive persistent structural evolution. Learning operates only over transitions admitted by the underlying kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) process, preserving event legality, state evolution, and physical time. Across BCC Fe-Cu precipitation, FCC Ni-Cr-Al ordering, and HCP Zr-H interstitial transport, restoring kinetic context consistently advances persistent evolution while maintaining physical fidelity and transferring to unseen conditions. In irradiated reactor-pressure-vessel steel, this approach achieves up to 420-fold greater persistent evolution under matched event budgets. Combined with scalable execution, it successfully extends mechanism-resolved trajectories to service-year timescales across metre-scale heterogeneous domains.

title: When a Permitted Action Completes a Forbidden Workflow: Designing Consequence-Oriented Approval for LLM Agents
comment: Under Review at the 41st AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-27)
summary: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly ask people to approve consequential actions, yet an approval prompt shows only the next step. A request to send a file to an approved recipient can look harmless even when that file was assembled, several steps earlier, from data the user said must never leave. We call this a cumulative authorization failure and argue that it is an interaction design problem as much as a security problem. The evidence a reviewer needs is spread across the trajectory, and listing it in time order leaves the reviewer to reconstruct the causal chain. We present the Cumulative Consent Ledger (CCL), an approval interface built on four design principles that restate the user's intent, bind the review to the exact action, compose the cumulative consequence, and keep every claim checkable. A trusted monitor that tracks artifact lineage supplies the evidence. In a between-subjects study with 80 participants and 960 approval decisions, CCL was associated with fewer unsafe approvals than an evidence-matched chronological log (24.2% vs. 32.5%), higher comprehension, and faster decisions, although the adjusted difference in unsafe approvals remained uncertain (-7.9 points, 95% CrI [-19.7, 3.8]). In a system evaluation, the monitor detected 89.2% of 120 violating checkpoints and, used as an execution gate, reduced executed unsafe effects from 43.3% to 5.0% for one agent at a small cost to benign completion. We derive implications for designing consent around consequences rather than individual calls.

title: Beyond Unit Tests: Path-Aware Rubric-Guided LLM Autograding of Notebooks
summary: Jupyter notebooks support open-ended, multi-step assessments in which students build one logical flow across interdependent steps, combining code, written analysis, and generated outputs such as plots. These reflect authentic scientific practice but are hard to grade consistently, since students may make different yet equally valid choices at each step, so a later answer can only be judged in light of the choices a student made earlier. We present an LLM-based autograder for such flow-structured notebook questions. It generates a rubric from a reference solution, then applies a softening pass that relaxes criteria tied to the reference so legitimate alternative paths are not penalized. Each question group is graded in a single model call, so later answers are judged against the student's own earlier choices, using question-type tags and schema-constrained, low-temperature outputs. Evidence is scored multimodally: code, text, numerical outputs, and figures from code cells. We deployed the tool in a machine-learning course, integrated with Gradescope, with a pre-submission format check and prompt-injection defenses, and evaluate it both in that live course and against archived submissions graded by staff in earlier terms. We report agreement, cross-model variance, cost, student perceptions, and injection resilience. With low-temperature models, agreement with human scores is often strong, including on the open-ended items the design specifically targets, while run-to-run stability depends sharply on the model's temperature support.

title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails
summary: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.

title: EvoViM: Recursively Self-Evolving Visual Agents for Exploration with Deferred Queries
summary: Multimodal large language model (MLLM) agents have shown promising capabilities in task-oriented environments. However, they still struggle when queries are deferred until after exploration, requiring them to retain visual evidence before knowing which details will matter. We introduce EvoViM, a recursively self-evolving framework in which a frozen multimodal model turns its own interaction experience into one visual program for memory and skills. The program retains images and computes directly on pixels, and its operations decide how this evidence is used in each task. During memory evolution, the same model traces failures in its visual trajectories to the operations that lost or misused evidence and revises them. It also rewrites the notes and analysis tools that guide later revisions, which then build on earlier findings and skip changes that have already failed. We evaluate EvoViM with three multimodal models on six tasks covering visual matching, spatial recall, and sequential decision-making, including three tasks with deferred queries. Across the six tasks, EvoViM improves the average score over AutoMem, the strongest baseline in the main comparison, by 31.3-47.6 points on held-out episodes. Programs written once from the initial environment instructions perform substantially worse, highlighting the value of interaction experience in shaping how visual evidence is retained and used. Code and dataset are available at https://evovim.github.io/.

title: HiPPO Functional Memory: Coordinate-Queryable Attention for Irregular Time Series
summary: Irregular time series are recorded at nonuniform times and are often queried at other times: between observations, after the last one, or on a regular grid. Continuous-time models answer such queries by integrating latent dynamics, and time-aware attention models answer them by revisiting the observation tokens. We introduce HiPPO Functional Memory (HiPPO-FM), an attention operator that writes an irregular history into a rank-M function space with explicit time coordinates. Masked self-attention first exchanges content among the observations; the updated values are then contracted against kernel-smoothed HiPPO-Legendre features and solved through a regularized Gram matrix, so the retained coefficients define a function that is read at any time through the same features. The write and read have the form of an interdomain sparse Gaussian-process mean: every readout lies in an M-dimensional reproducing-kernel subspace, and a pointwise bound separates the approximation error of this subspace from the error of the learned memory. Removing the functional memory from the encoder raises Spiral reconstruction RMSE 18-fold. The full model has the lowest error in 11 of 12 Spiral settings, the highest overall accuracy and best average rank on 20 irregular UEA datasets, the highest event-type accuracy on all five multi-type event benchmarks, and a 21% lower extrapolation MSE than CRU on PhysioNet. Because the memory has fixed rank, the state retained after encoding keeps a fixed size as the history grows and is 102 times smaller than a token cache at 1,024 observations.

title: Agent Money Benchmark: Can AI Agents Be Trusted to Spend Money?
summary: Giving an AI agent a wallet lets it buy data and services on a client's behalf. Trust then depends on how it spends money and what that spending achieves. We introduce Agent Money Benchmark (AMB) to test whether agents spend a client's money well, starting with purchases of information for financial decisions. We link seller quotes and payments to final answers, evaluating 12 models on 80 payment tasks with simulated sellers and 76 research questions using live data. Purchases settled in USDC on Solana mainnet via x402, a protocol for paying per web request. Three of the 12 models passed 79 of 80 payment tasks without payment or budget errors. Nine fell for a seller's trap at least once; repeat charges and above-list quotes accounted for 79% of scam events. We estimate waste from data and inference costs, counting failed payment tasks in full and research answers in proportion to missed points. With spending split equally between tracks, estimated waste ranged from \$21.0 per \$100 for Claude Fable 5.2 to \$70.8 for GPT-6 Luna.

title: PAMS: Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-tuning
summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization provides a computationally efficient approach to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), but conventional methods typically rely on isotropic perturbations that ignore the anisotropic structure of neural-network parameter spaces. We introduce Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace (PAMS), a ZO optimization framework that uses forward-pass activation statistics to construct structured, layer-wise perturbation geometries without computing gradients or forming dense curvature matrices. PAMS tracks a low-rank approximation of the dominant activation subspace and its associated spectrum online, and uses the spectrum to softly reweight perturbation variance while preserving exploration in directions outside the retained subspace. A trace normalization separates the perturbation geometry from its overall scale, enabling consistent perturbation magnitudes across layers. We show theoretically that the resulting perturbation covariance induces right-side preconditioning of the gradient of the corresponding Gaussian-smoothed objective. We further characterize the estimator's smoothing bias and second moment and derive a nonconvex convergence guarantee that captures the effects of the perturbation geometry and smoothing radius. The proposed low-rank tracking procedure requires $\mathcal{O}(n_l r)$ persistent memory for a layer with input dimension nl and retained rank r, avoiding the $\mathcal{O}(n_l^2)$ memory required by a dense activation covariance. Experiments on transformer-based language-model fine-tuning tasks across GLUE and SuperGLUE demonstrate that PAMS improves the effectiveness and stability of zeroth-order optimization while retaining its gradient-free and objective-evaluation-based advantages.

title: Internalized Experience: How Training Data Shapes Memory Formation in LLMs
summary: Parametric memory enables large language models (LLMs) to retain information from past experience and reuse it in subsequent tasks. Yet how training data supports the internalization of reusable task rules remains unclear. We introduce FSMem (Finite-State Machine Memory), a state-transition framework for constructing training data and studying how data content and organization shape memory formation. We evaluate rule reuse across synthetic worlds, classical planning, and code execution through valid-action identification and execution-outcome prediction, complemented by next-operation prediction in code. Our experiments reveal several systematic learning patterns. Under matched training conditions, even unchanged task rules become harder to internalize when learned alongside a larger variety of action types; by contrast, scaling the training data to provide broader state-action coverage generally improves rule learning. We further find that training at a single execution depth produces depth-specialized behavior, with models performing best when training and test executions have similar lengths. Motivated by this finding, we construct cumulative corpora that combine short and long trajectories, which can outperform long-trajectory-only training while using fewer training tokens. Together, these results demonstrate that the same task rules can be internalized differently depending on how execution experience is constructed, and that understanding these learning patterns can guide the design of more effective training data for parametric memory.

title: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
summary: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. Composed in one model, its modules for six BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) subtasks raise the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: at most 35.01) and that of Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. Against the unmodified model at the same precision, both composites leave the next-token distribution on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens unchanged (KL exactly 0), give identical answers on 15,845 items of five other Leaderboard tests and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The agent also writes exact multiplication up to 20 digits, running the model only up to 6 (100.0% on the absent lengths of the sealed test in both models; a LoRA with the same budget: at most 2.1%). Sets, rules and report sentences were sealed in git before the first session (manifests timestamped in Bitcoin), with dated amendments listed in Appendix D; a frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once. Verdicts (H5: tracking; H6: composite; H8: one pass vs. chain of thought; H9: fresh and rewritten instances; H10: side effects; H12: multiplication), on the preregistered sealed test, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H9 success, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success; Gemma-3-1B-it (H7: H5, H6, H8 and H9 in this model): H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H8 (tracking 3) success, H9 partial, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success. Not everything worked: 4 of 45 single modules show small side effects and 5 of 50 sessions hit the 12-hour limit without a module.

title: VeriLadder: A Multi-Agent Specification Refinement System for Tool-Verified Verilog Datasets
summary: Training data is a bottleneck in AI, especially for large language models (LLMs) that write Verilog, because register-transfer-level (RTL) code is rarely published and existing datasets mostly check code for syntax, not instruction correctness. This paper presents VeriLadder, a five-level Verilog dataset, and the multi-agent framework that builds it, in which LLM agents write and revise specifications, and EDA tools (a synthesizer and a formal equivalence checker) decide what is accepted. Its levels follow an engineer's checks. Level 1 labels designs from two large Verilog corpora, namely RTLCoder and PyraNet, with synthesis results, failure causes, critical warnings and post-synthesis metrics. 28% of RTLCoder designs fail synthesis and are kept as negatives. Level 2 grades each instruction on four specification qualities, and low grades predict failed rebuilds. Level 3 rewrites each instruction into a refined specification and accepts it only if an LLM from another model family, reading only that specification, writes a circuit formally equivalent to the original. This raises the share of rebuildable designs from 26.1% to 78.2%, keeping every failed specification with its counterexample. Levels 4 and 5 add verified paraphrases and one-fact variants, hard negatives that differ only in one behavior from the verified design. VeriLadder labels the synthesizability of 716,627 designs and, from RTLCoder, provides 11,247 refined specifications, 32,393 paraphrases and 8,397 one-fact variants. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on VeriLadder raises functional pass@1 from 31.7% to 50.0% on VerilogEval v2 and from 35.0% to 45.2% on RTLLM v2. The dataset and fine-tuned models are publicly available.

title: AMP-OD: Active Model Probing for Unsupervised Outlier Model Selection--Extended Version
comment: 25 pages. An extended version of "AMP-OD: Active Model Probing for Unsupervised Outlier Model Selection" accepted at KDD 2027
summary: Outlier detection is often deployed in fully unsupervised settings, where labels are unavailable and practitioners must choose a detector without direct performance feedback. Existing unsupervised outlier model selection methods predict detector quality from static meta-features and historical performance on meta-datasets, but they commit before observing how any detector behaves on the target dataset. We propose AMP-OD, an execution-conditioned probe-then-commit framework. AMP-OD runs a small number of inexpensive probe detectors, uses their score patterns as target-dataset evidence, and then selects a final detector from a larger candidate pool. To interpret unlabeled probe responses, we introduce a Leave-One-Out Family Probe Posterior (LOO-FPP), which converts probe score patterns into gated detector-family evidence while reducing self-validation in pseudo-label construction. AMP-OD further combines this evidence with historical reliability through a warm-start prior, a sequential probe/stop policy, and lower-confidence-bound arbitration. Extensive experiments and ablation studies show that detector responses provide useful evidence beyond static meta-features, with the LOO-FPP and conservative arbitration as key contributors.

title: Distilling Visual Agents from Limited Interaction Experience
summary: How much interaction experience is needed to distill a capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at fixed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four fixed trajectories raise a 4B student's success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to a 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a 9B extension further support the value of compact experience.

title: State of Mind: Learning and Evaluating World Models of Naturalistic Brain Dynamics
summary: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.

title: Mitigating Backdoors in Masked Diffusion Language Models
summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models because they can predict multiple tokens in parallel rather than generating tokens sequentially. However, recent studies have shown that MDLMs are vulnerable to backdoor attacks: when an input contains an attacker-chosen trigger, a backdoored model generates a targeted output, such as malicious code, while otherwise behaving normally. Despite this threat, backdoor defenses for MDLMs remain largely underexplored. We present UNMASK, the first defense framework for MDLMs that detects trigger-containing inputs, localizes the trigger tokens, and removes the backdoor from the compromised model. UNMASK exploits two fundamental properties of backdoor triggers, specificity and dominance, to assign a suspiciousness score to each input token. By leveraging two distinctive capabilities of MDLMs, parallel token prediction and token reconstruction at arbitrary positions, UNMASK computes these scores both effectively and efficiently. We further provide a theoretical analysis supporting the design of UNMASK. Evaluations across 40 settings spanning two attacks and four models show that UNMASK detects 99.3% of trigger-containing inputs at a 5% false-positive rate, substantially outperforming the strongest adapted baseline, which achieves 54.8%. UNMASK also achieves over 99% trigger-localization accuracy and reduces the average attack success rate from 95% to 1%, while largely preserving the model's utility on clean inputs.

title: DisSparse: Pipelined Top-$p$ Sparse Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
summary: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by the memory demands of the key-value (KV) cache, whose size scales linearly with context length. Dynamic sparse attention reduces this bottleneck by fetching and attending only to a critical subset of tokens. The dominant primitive in dynamic sparse attention research and deployment is fixed-budget top-$k$ selection, which is favored because its deterministic block count aligns with the static memory allocation that systems like vLLM rely on. Top-$k$ uses a fixed budget regardless of how attention mass is distributed across heads, layers, and decode steps, leading to either wasted bandwidth on heads with peaky attention or dropped context on heads with diffuse attention. Top-$p$ (nucleus) selection adapts naturally to this variation but has seen limited adoption in production serving systems due to two system-level challenges: variable block counts that break deterministic block allocation and computationally expensive selection kernels that exceed the cost of attention itself. We present DisSparse, a serving system that integrates top-$p$ sparse attention into vLLM end-to-end. DisSparse decouples block selection from the scheduler's critical path, hides selection latency behind layer computation via a two-stream pipeline, and introduces a single-pass histogram-based top-$p$ kernel. We further observe intra-block sparsity, the inflation of selection budgets caused by mixing high- and low-importance tokens within fixed-size KV cache blocks, and address it with a token relocation kernel guided by accumulated prefill attention scores. Across long- and medium-context benchmarks on multiple models, DisSparse achieves 1.17x to 1.80x speedup in sparsity analysis (block selection) over state-of-the-art top-$p$ methods with negligible accuracy loss and supports up to 8x larger maximum batch sizes than dense vLLM under the same memory budget.

title: Unlearning Model Identity: Ablating LoRA Weights from Question-Based Identity Tuning
summary: Large Language Models are trained on diverse corpora containing outputs from proprietary teacher models and provider-curated sources. Models subsequently inherit embedded self-identity traits, persistently asserting specific proprietary names. Service providers of open-weight models frequently require the removal of model identity for downstream applications, such as custom interfaces, without exposing provider affiliations to end-users. Effective identity modification is therefore critical for customized model alignment and deployment. This study proposes a method to localize parameter-level representations of self-identity within low-rank adaptation modules to perform targeted weight ablation. By generating probing questions designed to elicit self-naming outputs and fine-tuning the base model on these responses, the approach identifies and ablates high-magnitude weights within the parameter set. Experimental results demonstrate that distilled identity traits reside within a localized subset of low-rank weights, achieving a complete removal rate in Qwen3.5-2B and a 10% rate in Gemma4-E2B while preserving general task capabilities. These findings confirm that ablating top-tier adaptation weights suppresses distilled self-identification without compromising broader model performance.

title: SAFE-DRIFT: Data Selection for Supervised Fine-tuning with Controllable Off-Target Drifts
summary: We propose SAFE-DRIFT, a data-selection framework for supervised fine-tuning that improves a target capability while controlling unwanted drift in the model's other behaviors. We formalize this as a constrained optimization problem that maximizes alignment with the target gradient, subject to a budget on off-target drift which we quantify using the Fisher information of a reference distribution. Under this objective, the optimal, closed-form update is a damped natural-gradient step that downweights reference-sensitive directions. To estimate these high-dimensional gradients and work within the right geometry, we further derive a scalable algorithm that approximates the Fisher information and the target gradient in a shared low-dimensional subspace and analyze how entanglement of the target and reference task can affect the update. We evaluate SAFE-DRIFT against state-of-the-art data selection methods across diverse domains including coding and medical question answering, yielding competitive target performance while reducing degradation on specified off-target behaviors.

title: Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.

title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
summary: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $μ$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $μ$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $μ$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $μ$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

title: Improving the Improver: Semantic PID Control for Medical Agent Self-Improvement
summary: High-stakes vertical medical tasks, such as postoperative pathological staging and long-term survival prediction, demand multi-step clinical reasoning over heterogeneous evidence under weak supervision and high outcome uncertainty. While we first orchestrate CliAgent, a domain-tailored clinical agent workflow that systematically grounds predictions in multi-modal patient evidence, manually designed medical agents remain constrained by static, brittle rules. Moreover, existing recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods suffer from feedback ambiguity and severe development-set overfitting when evolving agents in high-noise medical domains. Focusing on improving the improver, we propose Semantic PID-RSI, an evidence-guided control-theoretic framework for medical agent self-improvement. Inspired by PID control, our improver evaluates candidate modification batches via three diagnostic roles: P isolates current clinical failure modes, I synthesizes longitudinal evidence from past trials, and D estimates response dynamics and regression risks (D-pre/D-post). Selected plans are compiled into behavior contracts for staged probing and independent adoption judging. Instantiated and validated on challenging oncology tasks (pT/pN staging and survival prognosis), evolving CliAgent with Semantic PID-RSI on a 3B-activated open-weight model achieves substantial gains (up to +6.27 C-index points), outperforming overfitting-prone RSI baselines and approaching the performance of frontier proprietary models (e.g., GPT-6 series) equipped with CliAgent.

title: Understanding and Mitigating the Fragility of Self-Rewarding Optimization
summary: Self-rewarding optimization (SRO) promises to improve language models by enabling them to generate their own reward signals. Yet when and how SRO succeeds or fails remains poorly understood. We reveal that SRO is fundamentally fragile: even seemingly benign perturbations to training prompts can corrupt the self-generated preference signal and trigger iterative collapse. We demonstrate this through two prompt-level attacks that serve as controlled stress tests: a Re-Ranking attack that concentrates training on prompts where self-reward diverges from an oracle, and a Preamble attack that learns short prefixes inflating self-reward without any gain in oracle quality. To explain why these attacks succeed, we introduce self-reward fidelity (SRF), a metric quantifying on-policy agreement between self-evaluated and oracle rewards. We show that SRF can serve as a diagnostic signal of self-supervision reliability, and that controlled SRF perturbations induce a phase-transition region: SRO improves when SRF remains sufficiently high, but collapses once SRF drops below a model- and task-dependent threshold. This analysis motivates Projection Decoupling Defense, which suppresses SRO update components along directions to which the reward generator is locally sensitive, improving SRO robustness under adversarial conditions. This work sheds light on the fragility of SRO and charts promising directions toward making it more robust.

title: DeCo: Decoupled Traffic State Modeling with Cross-Variable Coordination
summary: Accurate forecasts of traffic flow, occupancy, and speed are essential for congestion management and travel planning. These variables exhibit distinct spatiotemporal patterns, and their coupled dynamics characterize the evolution of traffic conditions, such as the onset and dissipation of congestion. Existing methods often either neglect this coupling or struggle to capture the distinct dynamics of all three variables within a unified model. In this paper, we propose DeCo, a decoupled traffic state modeling framework with cross-variable coordination for forecasting flow, occupancy, and speed. Specifically, DeCo first trains a dedicated forecaster for each variable to specialize in its unique spatiotemporal dynamics. It then estimates a residual correction for each forecast by jointly leveraging the predicted trajectories and recent observations of all three variables, thereby exploiting cross-variable coupling and mitigating systematic prediction errors. We extend the flow-only PeMS03 and PeMS07 benchmarks to all three variables on their original sensors and release the aligned data. Experiments on PeMS03, PeMS04, PeMS07, and PeMS08 show that DeCo achieves the lowest mean absolute error for every variable on every dataset, up to 4.9% below RAGC, the strongest baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/lixus7/DeCo.

title: DRAM: Memory-Efficient Muon via Rank Reallocation in Principal-Random Subspaces
summary: Memory-efficient Muon methods aim to reduce storage overhead while preserving strong performance, yet existing approaches compromise either convergence guarantees or practical efficiency. In this paper, we focus on subspace optimization for Muon, where the choice of subspace determines the gradient information retained for updating. To preserve dominant information while providing the coverage needed for stochastic convergence guarantees, we construct a principal-random subspace that combines leading singular directions of the stochastic gradient with random directions sampled from their orthogonal complement. Under a fixed rank budget, there is a trade-off between principal exploitation and complementary coverage, making rank allocation important for practical optimization. Our key observation is that the preferred balance shifts from principal-heavy early in training to random-heavy later. Motivated by this shift, we propose \dram, a memory-efficient Muon optimizer that reallocates principal and random ranks across stages while maintaining momentum and performing matrix-sign normalization entirely in the subspace. Theoretically, we establish convergence guarantees for general rank-allocation schedules with nondecreasing coverage factors, obtaining rates of $O(T^{-1/4})$ in the stochastic setting and $O(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting, with fixed allocation as a special case. Using a simple linear reallocation schedule, \dram achieves the best low-memory performance across three pre-training scales and nine fine-tuning settings.

title: Can Your AI Twin Meet People for You? It Can Hold a Conversation. But What Does It Need to Judge Like You?
summary: Should your AI twin go meet people on your behalf? We built LLM twins of 710 real people from their other conversations in the CANDOR corpus, sent them to meet each other in 5,680 simulated first conversations, and checked every rehearsal against what the real people said after meeting for real (355 held-out, participant-disjoint pairs, against baselines that include each person's rating history). The rehearsals work: a twin's conversation predicts real liking ($ρ$=0.277), carries information that questionnaires and rating history do not have (partial $ρ$=0.16 [0.05, 0.26]), and recovers most of what the same reader gets from the real conversation (0.321). Swap controls show that this signal travels through the conversation, not through the persona card. What, then, does a twin need to judge like you? Not your voice: making twins talk more like their owners, with person-specific activation steering and a LoRA trained on their own speech, did not help in a pre-specified test and lowered accuracy in an exploratory second round (-0.183 [-0.294, -0.066]). Nor simply your stated ratings: a persona-prompted twin that holds the conversation does not yet carry its owner's judgment, and when told its owner's past ratings it anchors on them instead of weighing them. Learning helps: a small appraisal head trained on other real conversations, which combines the twin's post-call answers with its owner's rating history, lifts rehearsal-based prediction above the history baseline out of fold (+0.059 [0.001, 0.115], against +0.022 without the twin's answers; pre-specified primary contrast +0.056 [-0.001, 0.111]). We propose an attribution protocol for twin-based social simulation and identify learned appraisal as the component twins need next.

title: Bridging Teacher-Student Capability Gaps with Recurrent Computation
summary: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from large language models to smaller students, yet stronger teachers do not always yield better students. Recent studies report diminishing or even negative returns from teacher scaling. We hypothesize that these limitations arise in part from insufficient student capacity to absorb the teacher's knowledge. We therefore investigate loop and recurrent computation as a way to expand the student's effective capacity by modifying its computation graph while keeping the backbone parameter count fixed. Under teacher-forced KD during pretraining, weight-shared looping improves performance but retains teacher-size saturation, whereas cross-token recurrence avoids the observed reversal with larger teachers. In mathematical post-training under both teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation (OPD), recurrent students scale better with increasing teacher size than looped and vanilla LLMs do. Crucially, we show that a pretrained LLM can be readily fine-tuned into a looped or recurrent architecture jointly with OPD, without repeating pretraining. Our recurrent Qwen model improves with larger teachers and consistently outperforms looped and vanilla LLMs. This suggests a new post-training paradigm that integrates architectural conversion into distillation, avoiding a separate conversion stage while substantially improving student performance and maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.

title: Beyond Single-Turn Privacy: Training-Data Leakage in Conversational RAG
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is known to reduce training-data leakage in single-turn interactions, but whether this protection persists over multi-turn conversations is unclear. We introduce CRELT (Conversational RAG Extraction Leakage Trajectory), a reusable framework that tracks, turn by turn, the real contact details from the training data that a RAG system discloses. CRELT separates retrieval, conversation history, and attack strategy through a full-factorial design, uses a retrieval corpus verified to contain none of the target PII, and counts an item as leaked only when it is absent from the model input at the turn it is produced. In our main experiment, this criterion excludes 29-53% of raw matches that were already present in the input. Across GPT-J-6B, Pythia-6.9B, and Pythia-12B, targeting real Enron contact details, retrieval reduces disclosure under both full and cleared history, consistent with prior single-turn results. A length-matched control with random passages reproduces 91-99.5% of this reduction under cleared history and 47-78% under full history, so much of it comes from the added context rather than from what is retrieved. With retrieval enabled, however, retaining full conversation history increases disclosure by a factor of 3.6-4.9, while retaining only one previous turn already restores disclosure to approximately the full-history level. With retrieval, clearing the history reduces disclosure by 72-79%, but does not eliminate it. These results show that single-turn privacy audits can substantially underestimate training-data leakage in conversational RAG systems and that conversation-history policy is a critical dimension of privacy evaluation.

title: BitShare: Sensitivity-Aware Binning and Bit Sharing for Compacting LLM Weight Storage
summary: Decoding with large language models at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, so the bits stored per weight largely set its cost. Group-wise integer quantization stores every weight of a group at the same precision, although the input channels of a group differ in sensitivity. We present BITSHARE, a codebook-free weight format that keeps the integer grid and the dequantizer of group-wise quantization but varies precision within each group. Sensitivity-aware binning places the channels of each group into three bins at fixed positions, and static bit sharing with optimal bit-value allocation lets the less sensitive weights share their lower bits, each stored once per group or once per pair of weights. A sharing-aware version of GPTQ chooses every stored value, with no fine-tuning and no codebook. BITSHARE has two modes. BITSHARE-U gives every group the same layout, so its decoder routes bits by fixed wiring, while BITSHARE-N chooses a layout per group within the same bit budget. With calibration on the Pile and at the same storage, both modes have lower perplexity than GPTQ at 3 and 2 bits on WikiText-2 and C4. At 2 bits across Llama-2 and Llama-3 models, BITSHARE-N lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by up to 70% against SliM-LLM and up to 35% against GPTAQ. At the 2-bit perplexity of SliM-LLM, BITSHARE-U stores 13.6-19.4% fewer bits per weight, cutting DRAM weight traffic by the same fraction. A verified hardware decoder implementation synthesized in SkyWater 130 nm reconstructs BITSHARE weights at the throughput of INT-n and SliM-LLM decoders.

title: DiscernBench: Evaluating Cooperative Discernment of LLM Agents in Institutional Settings
comment: 33 pages, 11 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB)
summary: The deployment of large language models in operational settings demands evaluation of judgment under institutional constraint. We introduce DiscernBench, a benchmark for evaluating cooperative discernment: the ability of an agent to determine whether to comply with, refuse, or escalate a request in an institutional setting. DiscernBench comprises scenarios derived from real-world incident reports across domains such as aviation, law enforcement, and emergency management. We evaluate eight LLMs across three decision-making configurations and analyze both final decisions and the intermediate judgments produced during multi-agent deliberation. Under disagreement, Final Responders exhibit model- and role-dependent aggregation patterns in which a lone specialist recommendation can disproportionately influence the collective decision, a phenomenon we term Minority-Signal Override. Role-specialized multi-agent deliberation raises average over-escalation from 3.79% under direct single-agent judgment to 28.27%, with the direction and magnitude of minority-signal influence varying substantially across models and specialist roles. These results reveal distinct collective decision behaviors that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone. Trustworthy multi-agent systems therefore require evaluating not only individual specialist reasoning, but also how conflicting judgments are transformed into collective decisions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Disha1001/DiscernBench.

title: Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement-learning agents shape the observations they encounter; consequently, detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) states requires analysing action-conditioned trajectories rather than treating inputs as independent samples. We propose Action-Conditioned Transition Irreversibility (ACTI), a detector that evaluates forward and backward transition likelihoods, calibrates this comparison against the in-distribution profile at each timestep, and smooths the score over a short window, using no future information. We tested ACTI across six environments and fifteen detectors within OOD-RL-Bench, using the four anomaly mechanisms that qualified in every environment, with ten policy replicates per environment. All primary metrics are matched-time: each score after anomaly onset is compared with a clean twin rollout's score at the same timestep. Our method secured the top macro matched-time AUROC, outperforming the dynamics-model baseline (PEDM), while scoring transitions roughly two orders of magnitude faster. Compared to the state-only variant, ACTI achieved a small but consistent AUROC gain and a shorter detection delay. The capacity-matched forward-only baseline, ACTI-Forward, secured a statistically significant advantage in AUPRC alongside a reduced detection delay. The discrepancy in AUROC did not reach statistical significance. Ablation studies suggest instead that performance improvements stem from action conditioning, calibration at each timestep, and smoothing of the transition-likelihood scores. Based on these results, we recommend using ACTI-Forward.

title: When do stored facts become available in looped transformers?
summary: Looped transformers do not acquire new knowledge during a forward pass. Prior work shows that they store as many bits in their weights as non-looped models. It remains unclear how recurrence makes this knowledge available during inference. We study this question using synthetic factual recall and multi-hop reasoning, measuring depth-resolved readable information in bits with native readouts and tuned lenses. Under final-loop supervision, single-hop facts become readable progressively: heavier memorization loads delay retrieval despite comparable final readable information. Untied baselines of equal unrolled depth concentrate retrieval near the end of their stacks, whereas looped models expose facts earlier. This delay is not intrinsic to the tested recall tasks: training with supervision and depth-specific readouts at every loop makes near-final information readable after the first loop in all tested configurations. Representational analysis shows value-related structure emerging within states organized by the query key. We then study multi-hop chains whose facts are stored in the weights rather than given in the prompt. Intermediate entities become decodable in chain order, and aligned transitions show next-entity structure developing while current-entity structure remains dominant. Interventions in a released six-recurrence model establish a causal role for these representations. Counterfactual replacements of a probe-defined entity component at a single prompt position redirect downstream bridge entities and the final answer. Conversely, replacements from queries that reach the same entity through different preceding relations, preserving the remaining relation suffix, retain the original answer in over 99.5\% of tested cases. These results distinguish a training-dependent schedule for factual recall from the causal role of retrieved-entity representations in subsequent composition.

title: Interpreting Diffusion Model Activations in Natural Language
summary: Interpreting the intermediate activations of diffusion models (DMs) is key to understanding how they generate images. Existing interpretability methods for DMs provide limited support for open-ended interrogation, making it difficult to extract human-interpretable insights. We extend LatentQA, the task of answering natural-language questions about Large Language Model activations, to DM activations. We introduce the Diffusion-specific Activation Oracle (DAO), which translates DM activations into natural-language answers to open-ended questions about the ongoing generation.
