Our experiments show that DAO can effectively describe the content of the final image from activations at early denoising steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that DAO captures the structure of the DM's activation space well enough to steer image generation toward target attributes. Furthermore, we show that attribution patching through DAO identifies DM components that contribute to visual attributes specified in natural language. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/yamanoko/dao/tree/main}{here}.

title: Improving semantic equivalence in research-level math formalization
comment: Accepted at the 6th Math-AI workshop at NeurIPS'26
summary: Formalizing mathematics in Lean is never a word-for-word translation of a paper: a Lean formalization changes definitions, strengthens hypotheses, splits arguments, and adds lemmas the paper never mentions. It stands to reason that a model that is good at autoformalization must be a good predictor of how a natural language source must differ from its faithful Lean formalization. With that in mind, we collect 4{,}076 audited examples of such changes from 832 Lean projects that formalize research-level mathematics, and use them to ask a practical question: how well can a model \emph{write} Lean inside a real research-level project that may contain tens of thousands of lines of code, and does training on discrepancies between natural language sources and their faithful Lean formalizations help? Our training set consists of 3{,}431 tasks from 141 repositories, and the test set consists of 645 tasks from the remaining 27 repositories. Training on in-project Lean nearly doubles complete proofs ($11\% \to 20\%$) and raises the share of statements in gold agreement with the project's own formalization by nearly a third ($30\%$ to $39\%$). The gain comes from the pairs themselves: an adapter trained only to predict how the Lean will differ, or a model told the difference in advance, barely helps. Training on where formalizations depart from their sources is thus an effective way of improving semantic equivalence in research-level formalization.

title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
summary: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $Ω(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $η=1/H$ requires $Ω(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

title: Does a Frontier Large Language Model Know What It Can Solve? A 100-Conjecture Calibration Study
comment: Accepted at the 6th AI-Math Workshop at NeurIPS'26
summary: How does confidence correlate with actual performance in large language models, when attacking open research-level math problems? We address this question by studying the performance of ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Ultra on a set of 100 open conjectures in geometric analysis. By construction, the model first selected open problems in geometric analysis that it assessed that it had at least a 50\% chance of proving or disproving, and then assigned a probability of success to each question. 13 questions were then excluded after an audit, and the model was asked to resolve the remaining 87 problems. Its mean stated resolution probability was $0.617$, versus an observed rate of $0.103$ (Brier score $0.351$, ECE $0.513$), thereby demonstrating that the model was systematically over-confident in its self-assessment. However, the scores retained ranking signal (AUROC $0.714$). The model was highly overconfident in probability magnitude but did more often than not assign a high probability of success to the problems that it did resolve, than the problems that it did not. Hence, its probabilities were numerically mis-calibrated but directionally correct. All proofs have been formalized in Lean, thereby verifying correctness, and have been run through a semantic equivalence pipeline to ensure semantic equivalence between the formalized and informal statements. These are exploratory campaign outcomes, not fixed-budget success probabilities. The certificates prove formal statements; for a couple of questions, some geometric inputs are assumed in the lean proofs.

title: Aegis: A Conversational Prototype for Lung Cancer Risk Information and Follow-up
comment: 30 pages, including 12 pages of main text and references and 18 pages of supplementary material; 27 references. All authors contributed equally and share first authorship
summary: Collecting self-reported risk information and maintaining continuity between assessment, explanation, and follow-up are practical components of a lung cancer screening workflow. We present Aegis, a browser-based research prototype that combines a conversational questionnaire, rule-based risk categorization, downloadable reports, retrieval-augmented health information, and doctor-user communication. A session-oriented controller manages question progression and clarification, while a language model assists with answer validation. Structured responses are passed to a separate risk-analysis module, and reports are linked to user and session records through Firebase services. The project adopts a multi-agent design that separates information collection, validation, assessment, and report generation. Its documented verification scope comprises 45 functional test specifications covering account management, questionnaire interaction, reporting, doctor-side review, and consultation. The available evaluation describes workflow behavior qualitatively; it provides no per-case execution results, clinical cohort, predictive-performance measurements, or comparative experiments. We therefore present Aegis as an engineering prototype for organizing risk information and follow-up, with clinical validity and the benefits of its agent-based design remaining unestablished. The paper describes the implementation, distinguishes implemented workflows from incomplete extensions, and identifies the evidence required for reproducible and clinically meaningful evaluation.

title: EA-Bench: Measuring information and action efficiency under imperfect instructions
summary: Personal agents help users complete everyday work across digital applications. Many standard benchmarks assume that users provide sufficient information to solve a task. However, agents often encounter incomplete, distracting, or inconsistent information in practice. To systematically study agent inefficiency under such imperfect information, we introduce Efficient Action (EA)-Bench, which evaluates both tool calls and user interactions in work-related tasks. To our knowledge, it is the first benchmark to jointly evaluate tool-call efficiency and user-interaction efficiency under controlled missing, redundant, and conflicting information. We construct 63 base-task instances adapted from existing work-related benchmarks. To guide perturbation design and quantify task requirements, we represent workflows as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and examine node-level dependencies to identify where information can be withheld, contradicted, or supplemented with distractors. We use a two-stage validation process combining AI-assisted checks with expert screening to select 232 conditions from 792 initial candidates. We organize these tasks into Easy and Hard tracks by task complexity. Experiments show that imperfect information can reduce accuracy and increase tool-use and user-interaction costs. More concerning, several models obtain apparently correct outcomes by guessing user-specific values without confirmation, revealing potential execution unreliability in current models under imperfect user information.

title: Stein Guidance without Gradients: Discretization Uniform Diffusion Inference Time Scaling beyond Particle SMC
summary: Reward-guided diffusion requires effective steering and correction of the bias introduced by approximate value functions. A Brownian example shows that SMC with full multinomial resampling at every step can require particle counts to grow linearly with guidance depth to maintain accuracy. We propose Stein Guidance, which combines derivative-free guidance with whole-path independence Metropolis-Hastings correction. Value-weighted selection from centered Gaussian candidates approximates gradient guidance in expectation, using as few as two queries per step. Centering stabilizes the local normalizer estimates, and the same queries yield an explicit path weight for correction. Under uniform value and spatial regularity bounds, we prove superpolynomial decay of finite-grid total variation error in the number of MH updates, with constants that do not grow with guidance depth. The error prefactor tends to zero as the value functions approach exact Doob values and the time grid is refined.

title: Guarding with Judgment: Learning to Intervene for Multimodal Safety
summary: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help requires distinguishing an established hazard from a condition that still needs verification, a distinction that binary safety labels leave unspecified. We formulate this decision through four actions: allow, warn, review, and refuse. To ground these decisions in verifiable evidence, we build a corpus of 20,126 training audits and the JudiBench benchmark, connecting each action to diagnostic judgments, source evidence, and controlled context changes. Our guard, JudiAct, separately states what the source establishes, what condition governs the help, and how the rules apply. It then checks these three brief review items against the original inputs to predict diagnostic labels and a handling action. Supervised training learns individual judgments while comparing label assignments across related cases. A second stage swaps one review item at a time, using the resulting audit feedback to refine review generation. On JudiBench, JudiAct improves request and answer Macro-F1 by more than 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone. Across nine public benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art guards on the mean delivered-answer score in both pre-generation and post-generation settings, cutting MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.

title: Physical regime changes expose formula misuse in large language models
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information appended. Code and data: https://github.com/acodercat/AtmosRegime
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for scientific computing across the Earth and environmental sciences, but problems in these fields often involve distinct physical regimes. LLMs may fail to recognize these regime-dependent constraints, applying formulas outside their domains of validity and producing plausible but physically incorrect results. We systematically investigate these failures through controlled experiments and assess whether post-training can improve regime-aware reasoning. Across 72 physical mechanisms, we find frontier LLMs frequently misapply formulas outside their regimes of validity, reducing accuracy by 13-57 percentage points. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards enables Qwen3.5-9B to match DeepSeek V4 Flash (284B) on regime-dependent tasks, but its effectiveness is limited by the formulas available in the base model. Combining supervised fine-tuning on a few worked examples with reinforcement learning improves accuracy by 61 percentage points, while distillation from a teacher supplied with the correct formula raises accuracy from 0% to 71%.

title: FormaFin: Verifiable Financial Analysis with Solver-Guided Reinforcement Learning
summary: Formally verifying financial analyses generated by large language models (LLMs) remains challenging as financial rules are largely expressed in natural language and rarely have corresponding formal specifications. Training language models to formalize these rules is hindered by the scarcity of labeled data and reliable training signals, while confidential financial data favor small models that run locally. We introduce FormaFin, a framework that trains small open language models to translate financial rules into reusable SMT formulas. FormaFin integrates teacher distillation with reinforcement learning using an SMT solver to compute rewards from numerical thresholds stated in financial rules. We evaluate FormaFin on corporate loan monitoring, in which lenders check borrowers' financial figures against loan agreements. To evaluate our framework, we curate \bench{}, a benchmark containing 143 loan agreements and 2,527 questions covering compliance, earnings cushion, and debt capacity. Our results show that a 7B formalizer achieves 94.8\% accuracy, outperforming open LLMs up to ten times larger. Across three model families, accuracy ranges from 92.6 to 96.8\%. Our framework also detects 95.6 to 99.7\% of errors in other LLMs' financial analyses. We make FormaFin and \bench{} publicly available.

title: Peel, Don't Whack: Partial Coverage, Imperfect Validators, and Intervention Based Shortcut Mitigation
summary:
Without group labels, shortcut mitigation increasingly relies on interventions : label-preserving edits, such as background or watermark replacement, that are proposed automatically and accepted by a validator. Invariance to a complete family of valid edits yields robustness, but in practice coverage is partial and validators err.
  We analyze both in a stylized linear model. For the population logistic solution and the max-margin limit of gradient descent, the decision on every shortcut-flip group follows one additive rule. Hence worst-group accuracy never decreases with coverage, while individual groups can provably degrade, a mechanism for the Whac-a-Mole effect; full coverage is not always needed. In the logistic regime the validator's false-accept rate must stay below a closed-form tolerance that grows with coverage. With noiseless training data, one false accept can make the max-margin solution ignore the core. In this model, sensitivity-based discovery removes shortcuts in decreasing salience. We also give a model-agnostic certificate, valid under content-independent validation, whose validator-error term comes from an audit.
  Simulations match the theory, and deep networks on synthetic and real images show the predicted Whac-a-Mole signs, monotone worst-group accuracy and validator fragility. The resulting procedure, Peel (Propose-Edit-Evaluate-Learn), can propose candidate edits from the model's own mistakes. Given an oracle library of the benchmarks' intervention operators, it selects the right ones and beats group-label methods on Waterbirds and UrbanCars. With fully generated edits, run end to end from three discovery seeds, it improves on empirical risk minimization (ERM) on five of six benchmarks but trails exact edits.

title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures. Project page: https://openraiser.github.io/StudioBench/ and code: https://github.com/openraiser/StudioBench . Equal contribution: Xinglong Xu, Yuxia Zhu. Corresponding authors: Asher Qin, Jingxuan Wei, Cheng Tan
summary: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.

title: CLAIR: Consistent LLM Adaptation via Index-free Reprogramming
summary: Time-series forecasting with pretrained large language models (LLMs) uses contextualized patch representations, raising the question of how to align them. Matching patches at the same temporal position is natural, but self-attention allows each patch state to incorporate information from elsewhere in the input window, suggesting that useful correspondences can extend across positions. This flexibility, however, does not necessarily translate into consistent forecasts: similar patch states may play different roles when used in their original temporal order. To address both issues, we propose CLAIR (Consistent LLM Adaptation via Index-free Reprogramming), a teacher-guided framework that combines patch-level transport alignment (PTA) and forecast-level consistency (FC). A clean-view exponential moving average (EMA) teacher guides a mildly perturbed student, with PTA establishing soft, representation-dependent correspondences and FC encouraging agreement at corresponding future steps. The forecasting head retains the original patch order. We test this combination through controlled comparisons: while PTA and index-wise alignment perform similarly without FC, PTA+FC under EMA supervision reduces horizon-averaged mean squared error (MSE) by 2.1% on ETTh1 and 2.6% on ETTm1 relative to Index+FC. The same preference for PTA+FC emerges in comparisons with alternative matching strategies on Weather and ETTh2. Beyond these controls, CLAIR achieves the lowest horizon-averaged MSE on five of six long-term benchmarks and the lowest aggregate overall weighted average (OWA) on M4 among evaluated methods, with competitive few-shot performance. As the teacher and transport are used only during training, inference requires only the student.

title: STRIDE: Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-Guided Skill Disclosure and Evolution for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Skill-augmented reinforcement learning enables LLM agents to reuse task-solving knowledge across episodes, but existing systems typically expose agents to a flat skill pool and update skills only from coarse, episode-level outcomes. This conflates two distinct uses of experience: a stable strategy that should frame the whole episode, and tactical know-how that should be retrieved only when the agent reaches a local execution gap. We propose STRIDE (Strategy-to-Tactics Retrieval-guided skIll Disclosure and Evolution), a framework that brings progressive skill disclosure into agentic reinforcement learning. STRIDE keeps the selected strategy visible as episode context, exposes a compact tactic menu, and loads full tactic content only after an explicit retrieval action. This interface turns each retrieval into an event-level credit unit: the same event provides process feedback for learning when to retrieve and supplies evidence for skill-bank evolution. On ALFWorld, STRIDE achieves a 92.7% average success rate with Qwen3-4B and a 94.9% average success rate with Qwen3-8B. On WebShop, it improves over the strongest reproduced skill-augmented baseline by 4.5 score points and 1.9 success-rate percentage points. These results show that skill reuse is most effective when persistent strategies preserve global task structure and tactics are disclosed only at local decision bottlenecks.

title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
comment: 33 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Code and Lean 4 proofs: https://github.com/researchbackup27-sudo/exact-littlestone-intervals
summary: The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.

title: When Do Better Visual World Models Make Better Plans? Decision-Aligned Selection for Latent Planning
comment: Supplementary material will be included in the next version
summary: Visual world models enable goal-conditioned planning by predicting the outcomes of candidate actions in latent space. However, planning depends on how well a model ranks candidates, whereas training optimizes how accurately it predicts each one. We identify the Decision-Relevant Residual (DRR), the part of the cost error that can reorder candidates, and show that the more training reduces the DRR, the more it improves selection (Spearman $ρ= 0.82$, vs. $0.61$ for prediction error). Building on this insight, we introduce Decision-Aligned Selection (DAS), a plug-in selection rule that scores candidates by the standardized consensus of several independently trained checkpoints, which averages out their checkpoint-specific residuals. Across two model families (LeWorldModel and DINO-WM) and five tasks, DAS selects better actions than single checkpoints in 12 of 18 configurations and outperforms training one model three times longer in 14 of 18. In closed loop, DAS improves success over single checkpoints in 6 of 9 pre-registered LeWM comparisons.

title: The Complexity of Oracle-Efficient Realizable Transductive Learning
summary: In realizable transductive online learning, the learner knows the entire sequence of $T$ instances in advance, and the labels are consistent with one of $N$ hypotheses. With explicit access to the hypothesis class, the halving algorithm makes at most $\log_2 N$ mistakes. Can a comparable guarantee be achieved using only polynomially many empirical risk minimization (ERM) queries? We answer this question negatively, even for a weighted-ERM oracle that optimizes arbitrary real-valued linear objectives and returns a complete maximizing hypothesis. For every fixed $β\in(0,1)$ and every randomized learner making polynomially many oracle queries, there exists a fixed realizable instance with exactly $N=2^{\lfloor T^β\rfloor}$ hypotheses on which the learner makes $Ω_β(\sqrt{T\log N})$ mistakes in expectation. This matches the agnostic-rate upper bound achieved by random playout using $O(T)$ oracle calls. The separation persists for much smaller classes as well: along a sequence with $\log N=Θ((\log T)^2)$, we establish a mistake lower bound of $\exp(Ω(\log T/\log\log T))$. Our main technical contribution is a composition lemma that combines two realizable prediction problems such that their mistake lower bounds add, up to a small loss, while their hypothesis class sizes grow only additively. Iterating this lemma yields a family of hard instances spanning the desired parameter regimes, establishing a sharp separation between information-theoretic and oracle-efficient mistake guarantees.

title: OmniDecisionBench: Evaluating and Benchmarking the Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models
summary: Multimodal System One models answer visual tasks with typed decisions and native probabilities, yet no holistic evaluation compares them with general VLMs or maps either class's capability boundaries. We introduce OmniDecisionBench, a holistic benchmark of multimodal System One models. Its main evaluation assigns 45 datasets (192,975 records) to five capability families and twelve primary angles across four typed interfaces, scoring accuracy and candidate-probability calibration. A validation layer adds three single-factor diagnostics varying visual presentation, textual evidence sufficiency, and target dataset. Across three System One models and two general VLMs, three regularities emerge. First, strengths depend on angle and metric: System One models lead discrete tasks overall with lower ECE15 on most perception, reading, and reasoning angles (Jev 1.14: 80.14% accuracy, 4.50% ECE15), while general VLMs lead ordinal grading and outperform Jev 1.14 among the three models tested on direct Box grounding. Second, multi-image and abstract reasoning bound every model, where confidence rather than accuracy separates them. Third, reliability shifts with the input: rendering only options nearly triples Jev 1.14's selective risk at nearly flat mean signed bias, and donor risk cutoffs often exceed target risk across unseen datasets and task families. OmniDecisionBench thus maps which model class suits each angle and where reliability ends. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/Glax147/OmniDecisionBench.

title: Operating-Condition Normalization in C-MAPSS: Matched Historical Baselines, Multi-Seed Robustness, and Prognostic-Score Trade-offs
summary: Operating-state changes can obscure turbofan degradation signals, but a reduction in remaining-useful-life (RUL) error after condition-wise standardization may reflect weaknesses of the comparison features instead of a unique benefit of normalization. A controlled retrospective audit examines NASA C-MAPSS FD002 and FD004 with engine-disjoint folds, raw condition identifiers, two constructions of causal history, early-life baselines, and continuous operating-setting correction. Ridge regression, random forests and XGBoost are compared under explicit training-engine-only fitting rules. The previously reported XGBoost FD004 terminal RMSE decreased from 30.38 to 29.08 cycles following six-condition standardization; however, raw sensor values accompanied by condition-matched histories and condition identifiers achieved 28.09 cycles, reversing the naive point estimate ranking, although the paired-engine interval spans zero. For FD002, normalized XGBoost reduced terminal RMSE yet increased the asymmetric NASA score (12,616 to 13,289). Additional model-seed, condition count, RUL-cap, grouped-validation and explanation checks test sensitivity rather than postulating a universally optimal representation. The six clusters reproduce known simulator operating regimes; no new condition discovery algorithm, causal diagnostic method, or field ready prognostic system is claimed. Since the official test endpoints were also used in earlier exploratory comparisons, all newly examined alternatives are reported as retrospective benchmark evidence, not as results from a pristine confirmatory holdout.

title: STEdgeFormer: MCU and NPU Deployable Transformer Architecture
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, Neurips 2026 workshop- SLM Agents
summary: Transformer-based sequence models have achieved strong performance in language and time-series modeling, but self-attention remains computationally and memory intensive for deployment on resource-constrained edge accelerators. We propose STEdgeFormer, a lightweight, hardware-aware sequence architecture designed for efficient execution on embedded neural accelerators. STEdgeFormer combines polynomial mixture layers and DyT normalization with an accelerator-aware causal memory block, replacing pairwise self-attention with compact causal aggregation. On TinyStories, the fully NPU-supported STEdgeFormer (MW) achieves a perplexity of 7.39 with 4.12M parameters and 6.51 MB RAM, with an end-to-end latency of 40 ms. In comparison, the standard 4.12M-parameter configuration achieves a lower perplexity of 6.79 but requires CPU fallback for unsupported operators, resulting in 1450 ms latency. Vanilla Transformer, on the other hand, achieves a perplexity score of 5.71 using a 4.40M-parameter model, but it cannot be deployed on the hardware. On downstream tasks, STEdgeFormer achieves 94% accuracy on ECG5000 and 93% accuracy on Speech Commands with 1.39M parameters. These results demonstrate that hardware-aware architectural choices and operator compatibility can have a substantial impact on practical inference latency, beyond model size and task accuracy alone. Rather than targeting state-of-the-art accuracy on individual benchmarks, STEdgeFormer is designed to provide a deployable sequence modeling architecture under the memory, computational, and operator constraints of embedded neural accelerators.

title: Pretraining Representation Lottery Determines Fine-tuning Generalization
summary: Large scale pretraining (PT) followed by fine-tuning (FT) is the central paradigm of modern deep learning, yet how PT shapes FT generalization remains poorly understood. We use a synthetic setup in which the ground-truth concept geometry of entities is known, as a controlled testbed to study how representational geometry affects model behavior and how PT representations determine FT generalization. We first show that models differing only in training seed can closely match in PT loss yet vary substantially in FT generalization. We hypothesize that a representational lottery underlies this phenomenon: the random seed dependent geometry formed during PT determines what FT can reach. We confirm this causally. First, injecting the ground-truth concept geometry into the model yields near-ceiling FT generalization, showing that good representations directly drive generalization. Then, distilling a lucky seed's learned representation into an unlucky seed unlocks FT generalization, while distilling the same model's behavior does not. Furthermore, representation distillation can merge entities that never interacted during PT, which FT alone cannot. Finally, we show that regularizing representational drift during FT enables naturalistic learning: only models with good representations learn the task, and they generalize, while models with poor representations fail to fit it. Under plain FT, by contrast, models with poor representations fit the training objective by reshaping their pretrained representations. We reproduce the distillation result in Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M, each pretrained multiple times with different random seeds, and show that the transferable representation lives in the deep layers at both scales. Overall, PT acts as a lottery over representations, and the representation a model draws determines how it adapts during FT in a way that behavior alone does not explain.

title: PruneNAS: Constraint Aware Neural Architecture Search based Pruning
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, British Machine Vision Conference, Lancaster, 2026
summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has achieved state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks, but its high computational cost remains a major barrier. We introduce PruneNAS, a novel framework that integrates structured pruning into NAS to efficiently explore high-performing architectures while leveraging pretrained models. Unlike conventional NAS methods that train each candidate from scratch, PruneNAS generates a candidate pool by pruning pretrained networks at multiple granularity levels and formulates the selection as a global optimization problem using training-free importance metrics. This approach enables rapid evaluation of candidate architectures under strict resource constraints, dramatically reducing search time from hundreds of GPU hours to mere minutes. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that PruneNAS discovers compact, high-accuracy architectures that nearly halve the computational cost (MACs) of prior methods on ResNet-50, while also showing strong generalization on object detection tasks with YOLO. Our method bridges structured pruning and NAS, offering a practical solution for resource-constrained model deployment.

title: Joint Client Scheduling and Resource Allocation for Optimal Federated Learning over Wireless Networks
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Revised author-prepared version of a paper accepted and presented at IEEE FLTA 2026
summary: Federated learning often relies on partial client participation because full participation is costly in cross-device wireless systems with limited uplink resources, heterogeneous channel conditions, energy constraints, and strict upload deadlines. However, partial participation introduces sampling variance, causing the sampled update to deviate from the full-participation update. Existing optimal client sampling methods reduce this variance but usually rely on simplified client-count budgets, while wireless-aware scheduling methods account for communication constraints but do not directly optimize sampling variance. This paper proposes resource-aware optimal client sampling (RAOCS), a unified variance-minimizing client scheduling framework under uplink resource-block, round deadline, update-information, and energy constraints. The resulting problem admits a capped water-filling solution that balances client update importance, wireless resource cost, and energy feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that RAOCS achieves accuracy comparable to that of OCS while reducing the average upload time per iteration by more than a factor of 252.

title: When Wrong Answers Remain Unsettled: Failure Dynamics in Recurrent Reasoners
summary: When a recurrent reasoner returns a wrong answer, is its computation finished or merely stopped? We test this on a trained Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM; 27M parameters, Sudoku-Extreme) by running the recurrence for one more inference budget and comparing with an unperturbed control. Solved answers persist (0.95 of 512 endpoints). Wrong answers mostly do not: 0.42 of near-miss answers (n=170) and 0.18 of all 512 wrong endpoints keep their answer. Perturbations from 0.05x to 20x the terminal-update scale barely change these rates, so the measurement reflects continued recurrence, not noise sensitivity. The solved-above-wrong ordering also holds in five further settings (a second seed, TRM, Maze, GRAM-guided TRM, N-Queens), but a fixed 1/2 persistence threshold does not, and neither do HRM's endpoint-spectrum and fast-versus-slow predictability patterns, which are not universal diagnostics. Perturb-and-reselect (known from prior work) is consistent with this: frozen noise gains 4.8 accuracy points (197 gained, 2 lost), but compute-matched extended depth gains 5.6 and Sudoku symmetry augmentation 34.6, so noise is not the best use of the budget. Conclusions are limited to finite horizons and one primary HRM checkpoint; they do not exclude asymptotic attractors.

title: ArrythML-II: An Optimized TinyML Framework for ECG Arrhythmia Detection and Multi-Class Beat Classification on Wearable Devices
summary: This paper presents ArrythML-II, an optimized TinyML framework for on-device ECG arrhythmia detection and multi-class beat classification on wearable platforms. A systematic hyperparameter optimization framework is developed to identify compact autoencoder architectures for binary ECG arrhythmia detection. A custom scoring mechanism jointly considers detection performance, reconstruction-error thresholds, and model size to guide architecture selection. The framework is further extended to six-class ECG beat classification using a lightweight classifier derived from the optimized autoencoder architecture. Both models are INT8 quantized and deployed using TensorFlow Lite Micro on a custom-developed, battery-operated, single-lead ECG device based on the PSoC~6 microcontroller. The deployed autoencoder and classifier have model sizes of approximately 44~KB and 22~KB, respectively, with end-to-end processing times of 5.1~ms and 4.7~ms per ECG segment. Model inference accounts for 3.95~ms and 1.38~ms of these processing times, respectively. In the refined arrhythmia detection evaluation using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, the autoencoder achieved an accuracy of 84.76\%, precision of 82.68\%, and recall of 77.99\%. The multi-class classifier achieved 82.29\% accuracy, weighted precision of 90.18\%, and weighted recall of 82.29\%. Beyond offline model evaluation, the wearable platform is validated using preloaded ECG segments, live ECG signals, and an ESP32-S3-based ECG emulator that replays annotated MIT-BIH recordings as analog waveforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating optimized TinyML models into wearable platforms for real-time ECG analysis.

title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.

title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Generative AI for Health (GenAI4Health) Workshop
summary: Synthetic electronic health record (EHR) generation is increasingly adopting large autoregressive models, yet privacy evaluation has not kept pace, relying heavily on similarity-based heuristics and aggregate metrics that can obscure patient-specific memorisation. We argue that these models should additionally undergo LLM-style memorisation audits at the level of individual patient records. We support this position by comparing membership-inference evaluations across four prominent autoregressive EHR generators, highlighting inconsistent evaluation practices in patient representations and attack procedures. We evaluate trajectory reconstruction from partial context and introduce randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorised associations from clinical generalisation. We examine these methods in a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, creating a controlled setting in which memorisation should be readily detectable. The model systematically recovers training patients' canaries, and their trajectory reconstruction approaches perfect accuracy with increasing context. Held-out patients show no systematic canary recovery, while reconstruction remains low and improves only marginally with additional context. These experiments establish a positive-control baseline for further evaluation of these methods in realistically trained models.

title: Do You Even Know What I Want? Improving LLMs Ability to Detect Hidden User Intent
summary: As with conventional AI agents, a common source of misalignment between Large Language Models (LLMs) and their human users is misspecified goals. Often, this happens when the human has skewed beliefs about the system's model and provides it with information that causes behavior different from what they expected, with potentially unwanted side effects. To ensure goal alignment, one solution would be for the LLM to ask the human questions about their objectives. However, it has been well-documented that LLMs most often provide default responses to user requests rather than try and ask questions to clarify their true intent. In this paper, we address these challenges by adapting a novel formulation for the objective misspecification problem to work with LLMs. We then test if LLMs that are prompted to ask questions about a user's true underlying objectives are better at identifying them compared to those that do not. We evaluate our method using four state-of-the-art LLMs tested on five standard IPC domains, showing that for some domains, asking questions greatly improved model performance.

title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.

title: The Retry Tax: Why Static Same-Task Retries Can Cost More per Completion
summary: Retrying an agent after failure can complete more tasks while increasing the cost per completion. We study a static policy that stops at verified success or an attempt cap and otherwise resets the original prompt and workspace without passing feedback to the next request. Under stationary task success probabilities, independent attempts conditional on the task, and a common attempt cost, easier tasks tend to succeed earlier. When task success probabilities differ, the unresolved mix shifts toward harder tasks. Specializing classical survivor selection, we show that cost per completion is at least as high as in one-shot serving and that marginal cost per additional completion is nondecreasing wherever the completion increments are positive. These are different quantities: one averages spending over all completions, while the other prices the completions added by another attempt. We then arrange each task's existing benchmark runs in different orders, stop each sequence at verified success or the attempt cap, and average the resulting completion and spending at each supported cap. For one OpenHands configuration, replay estimates completion of 59.7 percent with one attempt and 70.0 percent with four, while cost per completion rises from about USD 0.70 to USD 1.32. The recorded trade-off describes fixed configurations on the available tasks. Choosing a cap requires comparing the additional spending with the application's value for the additional completions.

title: Pixel Auto-Encoder: Reconstructing Language Model Activations Through Pixel Art
summary: Interpreting the high-dimensional internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a challenging problem. Recent approaches have explored translating these representations into human-understandable forms, particularly natural language. In this work, we explore the use of images as an alternative target modality for interpreting LLM activations. As a first step toward this goal, we introduce Pixel Auto-Encoder, which converts intermediate LLM activations into $32 \times 32$, 32-color pixel art and reconstructs them for subsequent computation within the model. By encouraging the intermediate representations to resemble predefined concept images, we investigate whether LLM activations can be expressed visually while preserving the model's language capabilities. We find that the model can produce target-aligned images for some concepts, and that replacing pixel representations with concept images can influence next-token predictions. However, we also observe a trade-off between visual alignment and language-model performance, as well as sensitivity to pixel-level changes that are difficult to interpret visually. These findings demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of image-based representations of LLM activations.

title: MVAgent: Per-Video Agents under Global Coordination for Multi-Video Understanding
summary: Multi-video understanding requires systems to combine evidence from different videos for cross-video reasoning. Answering such questions involves two kinds of decisions. Observation decisions must adapt to each video's content, whereas cross-video judgments require relating evidence from different videos based on the question. Most existing agents make both kinds of decisions in one controller, whose context accumulates observations from every video. We separate them in MVAgent, a training-free Multi-Video Understanding Agent framework with one LocalAgent per video. Each LocalAgent plans observations of its own video and keeps a private observation history. A GlobalAgent coordinates cross-video reasoning by instructing the LocalAgents and combining their reports with joint observation. We evaluate MVAgent on CVBench, MVU-Eval, and CrossVid, using three Qwen3.5 models of different sizes and GPT-6-sol. With Qwen3.5, our framework improves aggregate benchmark scores by 5.1 points on average over Single-pass inference with the same model and by 5.0 points over the strongest prior agent using the same model. With GPT-6-sol, the average gain over Single-pass inference with the same model is 4.3 points. On the same hardware, MVAgent also runs 1.8-2.7 times faster than prior agents of comparable size.

title: Hidden Sensitivity in LLM Pre-training: A Dynamic System View
summary: In Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, loss curves can conceal substantial instability, i.e., even small perturbations may lead to dramatically different predictions while leaving loss nearly unchanged. To investigate this phenomenon and reveal the underlying mechanisms, we first formulate LLM pre-training as a non-autonomous dynamical system that jointly evolves model weights and Adam optimizer states. Based on this formulation, we introduce a normalized sensitivity score in optimizer-relative coordinates to identify sensitive training checkpoints. At one such checkpoint, a weight perturbation of only 10^(-5) leads to 35.7% disagreement in top-1 predictions and 16.2% disagreement in benchmark answers after 200 training steps, with only 0.8% of greedy generations remaining identical despite similar validation losses. Furthermore, we find that perturbations to Adam's first and second moments induce comparably large effects, with similar sensitivity patterns observed in OLMo-1B. Finally, guided by our diagnostic, targeted stabilization reduces top-1 disagreement to 0.83% and increases generation exact match to 88.3%, at the cost of a 0.11-nat increase in validation loss. Our findings reveal a hidden form of optimizer-state-dependent sensitivity in LLM pre-training that conventional loss-based evaluations may overlook, while demonstrating its potential for diagnosis and mitigation.

title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
summary: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

title: AgriManager: A Framework and Benchmark for LLM-RL Generalization in Agricultural Management
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
summary: Agricultural management is heterogeneous along two axes. The first is distributional shift within a fixed task interface: weather, crops, and prices vary across years and locations while sensors, actions, and objective stay fixed. The second is structural shift across interfaces: different farms expose different observed variables, available actions, and management objectives. We formalize the second axis as schema shift: variation in the policy-facing schema $Σ= (Σ_O, Σ_A, Σ_R)$ between training and deployment. We test whether LLM-RL generalizes across both axes with AgriManager, to our knowledge the first framework that trains LLM policies with RL across multiple process-based crop simulators, unifying DSSAT, WOFOST, and Cycles. We design a three-tier generalization ladder: Tier 1 within-schema distributional shift, Tier 2 single-axis schema shift along $Σ_O / Σ_A / Σ_R$, Tier 3 compositional schema shift across simulators, all scored on a frozen held-out test suite with three training seeds per method. Within fixed schemas, Qwen3-4B trained by RL with explicit reasoning exceeds neural-network PPO trained with the same interaction budget; without reasoning, training stalls near no-action where the reward penalizes input use. Under single-axis schema shift, $Σ_O$ transfer needs decision-critical state, $Σ_A$ results are consistent with joint action-menu coverage, and with reasoning a policy trained on yield alone transfers to unseen objectives. Under compositional schema shift, single-source training mostly hurts zero-shot transfer across simulators, and a unified policy trained only on other combinations of the same components recovers about 86% of the gain of a specialist trained on the target combination on DSSAT and stays below the specialists on the WOFOST and Cycles profit targets. Project page: https://agrimanager-framework.github.io

title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
summary: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

title: Dynamic Model Merging with Multi-Layer Aggregated Routing Evidence
summary: Dynamic model merging aims to retain the efficiency of a unified model while better preserving task-specific expertise through input-dependent routing at both the task and head levels. However, even the routing components of the state-of-the-art approach remain limited: the task routing is highly sensitive to the choice of routing layer, whereas the head routing relies on simple max-logit competition. To address these limitations, we propose multi-layer aggregated routing evidence (MATE) as a unified mechanism for improving both task and head routing. Specifically, we first introduce a metric to quantify task routing separability across different layers. Empirical analysis of this metric reveals that different layers provide complementary evidence for identifying the tasks relevant to an input. Motivated by this observation, MATE selects multiple informative layers according to their routing separability and aggregates their layer-wise routing scores to produce a more robust signal that can be directly used for task selection. Moreover, we observe that this signal also encodes useful information about the suitability of the corresponding classification heads. This motivates us to further combine the MATE signal with the max-logit score to guide classification head selection. Extensive experiments on vision benchmarks demonstrate that MATE consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance.

title: Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies
summary: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $τ^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $τ^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

title: PhyMind: Physics-Informed Masked Autoencoding for EEG Foundation Models
summary: EEG foundation models are pre-trained almost exclusively with masked reconstruction through a free-form decoder, sometimes with hand-crafted spectral targets added, as in MANAS-2. We study what happens when that decoder is replaced by a generative forward model of EEG. PhyMind keeps a standard masked transformer encoder, but its decoder must explain the masked signal through 68 cortical regions, each driven by damped stochastic oscillators and an aperiodic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, projected to the recording's own montage by a fixed boundary-element lead field evaluated per derivation. Training combines masked reconstruction with a Whittle spectral likelihood, an oscillator-dynamics residual, a minimum-norm source prior and a penalised neural residual. In a controlled comparison (same encoder, data, steps and seed), the physics decoder produces encoder tokens whose spectral content is far more linearly decodable than with a masked-autoencoder decoder or with the MANAS-2 objective: mean R^2 on a token-level spectral probe with amplitude-normalised targets is 0.67/0.77/0.77 on three datasets, against 0.24/0.50/0.50 (MAE) and 0.48/0.67/0.66 (MANAS-2 objective), approaching the released 92.8M-parameter MANAS-2 (0.71/0.81/0.80). Downstream gains in the controlled setting are small (four-task mean balanced accuracy 56.6 vs. 53.8 for MAE frozen, 63.8 vs. 62.7 fine-tuned). Region-level features from the physics decoder raise frozen four-class motor-imagery accuracy by 7-14 points, so a 7.2M-parameter model pre-trained on 3k hours of open EEG is comparable to the released MANAS-2 with frozen features (63.0 vs. 61.6). After full fine-tuning, MANAS-2 remains better (66.8 vs. 65.4 for our best model). The inferred sources do not reproduce the lateralisation that a classical inverse solution finds in motor imagery, so we do not claim anatomical interpretability. Code and weights are released.

title: MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents
comment: 16 pages, including appendices. The MetaSkill library is provided as ancillary material
summary: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.

title: Interaction Retention and Output-Likelihood Training in Parallel Sampling
comment: 44 pages (35-page paper followed by a 9-page online appendix), 3 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Machine Learning Research
summary: Parallel samplers such as masked diffusion language models generate several coordinates per step from conditional marginals and randomize which coordinates are generated together, so even exact conditionals return a distorted distribution. We give an exact local account of this distortion. Around any full-support product law, the Gram operator of the sampler's response is diagonal in the interaction decomposition, and its eigenvalues are retention probabilities: the probability that an interaction has a unique latest-revealed coordinate. This retention spectrum determines the exact frontier between output accuracy and conditional calibration, its regularization path, and the population response of finite-mixture likelihood training. For pairwise interactions it yields a sharp dichotomy. Under homogeneous retention, output-likelihood training is equivalent to a single context gain; heterogeneous retention opens correction directions beyond any scalar, with an advantage bounded by an explicit heterogeneity gap. On binarized digits and MNIST, output-likelihood training within a heterogeneous schedule library lowers calibrated test negative log-likelihood in all twelve paired comparisons, and the gain survives pair-specific recalibration and a stronger path optimizer. For a frozen 169.6-million-parameter masked diffusion language model, serially normalized context gains are 1.070 and 1.056 at 8 and 16 rounds, against the predicted values 1.134 and 1.058.

title: DoppelVet: Comparative Safety Verification for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Self-evolving agents improve by retaining feedback as reusable memories or skills, but every mistaken approval can shape many future behaviors. Two updates can provide exactly the same evidence to a verifier yet produce opposite safety outcomes, so the verifier cannot distinguish them from that evidence alone. We introduce DoppelVet, a verification framework that checks proposed updates before they enter an agent's persistent state. Without access to safety labels, DoppelVet constructs an alternative that matches every signal used by the existing verifier. It replays both updates from the same state and directly compares their behaviors in both presentation orders before deciding whether to retain the candidate. We evaluate DoppelVet on DoppelVet-Grid and DoppelVet-Tool, covering executable programs and natural-language memories. Across nine open-weight and proprietary verifiers, DoppelVet raises mean harmful-update detection AUC from 0.762 to 0.940 on DoppelVet-Grid and from 0.681 to 0.826 on DoppelVet-Tool, outperforming VaG and AgentDoG 1.5. On DoppelVet-Grid, it reduces trajectories experiencing degradation from 30.39% to 0.43% over a ten-generation self-update loop and leaves no final degradation.

title: MolReJev: Decision Models Are In-Context Molecular Predictors
summary: Molecular prediction helps prioritize compounds for screening. Specialized predictors are trained for a fixed set of tasks, limiting cross-task generalization. Language models can condition on task descriptions and have recently shown promise in molecular prediction. However, generating answers token by token adds inference cost, and general-purpose models often lack task-specific molecular knowledge. We thus propose MolReJev, which combines Jev-style candidate scoring with in-context learning (ICL) on a language model. MolReJev retrieves similar labeled examples from existing task data and scores candidate labels jointly in one forward pass. ICL improves predictions from the released general-purpose Kev checkpoint and the separately trained MolReJev. For the trained model, gains span all evaluation groups, including held-out tasks, and extend to compounds absent from training. MolReJev generally outperforms MolecularGPT on matched evaluations and nearest-neighbor prediction with the same examples. With four examples, MolReJev and a trained text baseline achieve similar ROC-AUC, with higher measured throughput for MolReJev. These results show that decision models can serve as in-context molecular predictors for compounds, drug pairs, and reactions.

title: EMIP: Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform
summary: Experimental platforms that enable multiple participants to engage in spoken dialogue and perform physical actions concurrently in a shared environment are important for studying cooperation between humans and embodied AI agents. In this paper, we propose EMIP (Embodied Multi-Party Interaction Platform), a virtual environment platform built on Minecraft. Through an Internet-based client-server architecture, EMIP connects multiple humans and multiple AI agents to the same virtual environment and supports full-duplex speech communication and simultaneous physical interaction. It provides interfaces based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for environmental observation, physical action execution, and audio input and output, enabling researchers to develop their own agent control methods using large language models (LLMs). Additional features include centralized control of an agent group through a single EMIP agent client, collaborative object transportation by multiple agents, and experimental support functions such as recording and retrieving observation histories. By integrating these features into a reusable platform, EMIP aims to support research on human-human, human-agent, and agent-agent cooperation under different participant configurations and agent control methods. Usage examples illustrate concurrent speech and physical action, task coordination, and overlapping speech. The source code for the platform is publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AI-Humans-Lab/EMIP-Embodied-Multi-Party-Interaction-Platform).

title: Global Stability and Loss Convergence in Matrix Factorization
summary: We study the matrix factorization objective $\mathcal L(X,Y)=f(XY)$ for convex, twice continuously differentiable output losses with bounded and Lipschitz gradient and a minimizing set that is compact modulo specified input and output invariances. This includes the well-known cross entropy loss. We prove that a positive learning-rate threshold guarantees bounded parameters, summability of squared gradients, and convergence of the loss from every finite initialization. The proof constructs a quantity from the imbalance between parameter matrices that decreases over every step of the gradient descent trajectory.

title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
comment: Codes are publicly available at: https://github.com/JunboShen/SAE-Audit
summary: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

title: Stochastic non-metric MDS for noisy high-dimensional data
summary: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) constructs low-dimensional embeddings that approximate pairwise distances in a high-dimensional dataset. MDS exists in several flavors, with metric MDS approximating distances directly and non-metric MDS additionally optimizing for an arbitrary monotonic transformation of the high-dimensional distances. Empirically, metric MDS is known to suffer from the curse of dimensionality. Here we extend prior theoretical results for metric MDS on fully uninformative data to a more general case of finite, high-dimensional data with concentrated distances. We show that the metric MDS embeddings of such datasets stay distributionally close to the data-independent limit case. We then show that non-metric MDS is more robust to high-dimensional noise and can yield informative embeddings of such data. While existing implementations of non-metric MDS are slow, we develop a fast implementation using stochastic gradient descent in PyTorch. Using our implementation, we conduct an empirical study using multiple simulated and real-world datasets, including population-genomic and scRNA-seq data, and show that non-metric MDS can strongly outperform other methods in terms of global structure preservation.

title: Emotion-Aware and Context-Grounded Dialogue Agents for Personalized Video Game Interactions
summary: We present ChatNPC, a game companion that dynamically personalizes its responses in real time based on players' emotional shifts to enhance user immersion. The model integrates sequential data, leveraging the dynamic nature of streams to benefit from player information, spoken lines, and in-game context. We leverage recent progress in LLMs' tool-calling capabilities to extract vital information from memory and recognize potential constraints for accurate reasoning, thereby tackling the complexity of NPC conversation scenarios. The task is divided into a game sentinel-guided agent (SeGent), a memory capability, and a chat planning tool for reasoning instantiation. The approach uses a lightweight game template as an information framework, with relevant details and a thorough reasoning layout. We conduct extensive experiments on a newly developed game dataset for in-game context NPC dialogue and demonstrate that ChatNPC sequentially captures players' emotional shifts over time; responses are more naturalistic and human-like with appropriate conversational cues, pauses, and sighs; and utterances remain faithful to the dynamics of in-game context and player actions, supporting narrative continuity.

title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
summary: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.

title: Layer-Level Control of Language Model Execution in Agent Frameworks
summary: Agent frameworks typically orchestrate language models through prompt-and-response interfaces. We propose a harness design that exposes intermediate model states and layer-level execution controls to the agent runtime. By connecting state collection, policy fitting, and execution, the design enables policies to allocate computation within and across models based on intermediate states. We demonstrate the approach with a prototype that learns stitching bridges and state-conditioned execution policies from paired model states, then applies them during inference to select among continue, exit, and stitch. For dispatcher supervision, we select the least-computation action whose full-vocabulary next-token prediction matches the source model's full-depth prediction, using continue when neither early action matches. We train these components on a frozen proxy corpus of 5,000 typed-decision items authored using source texts sampled from WildChat conversations, then evaluate the prototype on JevBench measuring task accuracy, agreement with full-model predictions, and end-to-end latency including runtime overhead. Preliminary results show an approximately 15% reduction in mean latency while maintaining task accuracy comparable to full-model inference.

title: DoC: Learning to Defer or Commit for Timely, Accurate, and Stable Conversational Diagnosis Prediction
summary: Conversational diagnosis prediction requires accurate, early, and stable predictions from ongoing clinical dialogue, yet dialogue-level labels do not specify when to commit. We propose a two-phase framework for learning deferral and diagnosis decisions. First, iterative commitment-boundary estimation constructs Defer/diagnosis supervision without annotated commitment times. Second, Defer-aware supervised fine-tuning initializes a policy, refined through reinforcement learning with trajectory-level rewards for timeliness, first-commit accuracy, and post-commit stability. On EMSDialog and MediTOD, DoC commits early, achieving the highest first-commit accuracy among post-trained methods (76.7%/51.2%) and the lowest post-commit error overall (16.4%/48.3%).

title: Scalar Tuned Lens Summaries Offer Limited Incremental Value for Mid-Generation Abstention
summary: Mid-generation abstention aims to stop an unpromising response before spending its remaining computation budget. Intermediate transformer states may help predict eventual correctness, but whether scalar summaries of their vocabulary predictions add useful evidence is less clear. We compare Tuned Lens entropy and divergence features with final-state and raw intermediate-state probes under matched, causal evaluation. Across eight instruction-tuned models on MATH-500, raw intermediate states improve ranking, whereas scalar-only probes usually trail the final-state baseline. Scalar hybrids have positive exceptions, but their advantage over position-matched permutation controls is small. Cross-fitted residual comparisons further show that gains over a final-state probe need not require aligned scalar features. Actual stopping runs on two model sizes and two benchmarks reveal a separate accuracy--computation trade-off, with token savings overstating wall-time savings for scalar policies. The evidence supports a restricted empirical conclusion about these scalar features, not a general negative claim about intermediate representations.

title: Mirrored Min-of-K Training
summary: Min-of-K (MoK) training is widely used to train models that produce diverse outputs from random noise. For each target, it draws K outputs from the model and backpropagates only through the one closest to the target. However, MoK generally does not make the generated distribution match the data distribution. In this paper, we analyze the MoK bias across all values of K and show that tuning K shifts between failure modes, from mode dropping at small K to distribution flattening at large K. We further prove that every nontrivial loss based only on target-candidate distances fails to recover some data distribution, since these distances do not reveal how the candidates are placed relative to each other. Based on these analyses, we propose mirrored MoK (MMoK), a drop-in modification of MoK training that draws one extra sample from the model, applies the closest-candidate selection rule against it, and subtracts the resulting distance. Since this distance is measured between samples of the model, it provides additional information about how the candidates are placed relative to each other. We prove that MMoK can in principle recover data distributions that MoK cannot. We empirically validate MMoK on five scenarios, namely synthetic mixtures, pedestrian and vehicle trajectory prediction, tropical cyclone forecasting, robotic policy learning, and ambiguous medical image segmentation. The results confirm the effectiveness and generality of MMoK in both distribution learning and task performance.

title: Rethinking Closed-Ended Medical VLM Evaluation: From Stable Wrongness to Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity
summary: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring.
