In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.

title: AeroJEPA: A Two-Stage Framework for Aerosol Forecasting with Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning
summary: Aerosol forecasting requires integrating sparse ground observations and modeling meteorologically driven concentration evolution and spatial structure. However, analysis-initialized forecasts make limited explicit use of historical observations, while pointwise regression tends to smooth local variations and provides limited constraints on fine spatial structures. In this work, we propose AeroJEPA, a two-stage joint-embedding predictive framework for regional surface PM$_{2.5}$ forecasting. Specifically, Stage I fuses historical observations, model backgrounds, and meteorological information to predict an initial future state, meteorological conditions, and multi-scale structures. Morphology-guided encoding and joint-embedding predictive supervision support learning future spatial representations, supplementing concentration regression with structural constraints. Stage II uses predicted meteorology to guide state refinement and incorporates coarse- and fine-scale structures into state updates and decoding to generate the concentration field at a single future time step. Experiments show that AeroJEPA reduces gridded and independent-station RMSE by 17.23\% and 7.90\%, respectively, relative to PFGNet, while improving spatial consistency with analysis fields. In a 48 h recursive forecasting case study, AeroJEPA generally achieves lower RMSE and MAE than the numerical forecasts across the forecast period, indicating promising short- to medium-range forecasting performance.

title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
comment: Accepted at the AI for Science Workshop, NeurIPS 2026. 24 pages, 9 figures
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.

title: Aggregation Rules Induced by KL-Regularised Preference Dynamics on Networks
summary: We study agents that each align a model to their own preference data while observing one another, and ask which aggregation rule the resulting policies implement. Each round, an agent takes one KL-regularised step. The step involves a reference that the agent is penalised for leaving and a challenger against which its responses are compared, and each of the two may be the agent's own or an average over the agents it observes; attention need not be reciprocal. Aggregating the reference makes the rule collective. Agent $v$ then has the weight $π_v/β_v$, its share of the network's long-run attention divided by its temperature. If, in addition, the challenger is fixed, the agents concentrate on the response maximising $\sum_v(π_v/β_v)r_v(y)$, where $r_v$ is agent $v$'s reward, and the rule is cardinal. If the reference is fixed and the challenger aggregated, the agents' policies at a fixed point generally differ, and any weighted mean of them is an approximate maximal lottery whatever the weights, so the dynamics select no weighting. If both are aggregated, the rule is ordinal: averaged over rounds, the collective policy is a maximal lottery of the influence-weighted preference kernel, up to a slack that we bound. Where a collective rule exists, its weights depend only on the attention weights and the temperatures.

title: Beyond Fixed Prompt Configuration: Alternating Policy Learning for Adaptive Topology-Based Prompting in Few-Shot Graph Learning
summary: Graph Prompt Learning (GPL) adapts frozen pre-trained graph models to few-shot graph tasks through a small set of trainable prompts that encode task-specific information. Topology-based prompting instantiates this idea by augmenting an input graph with new prompt nodes and edges, yielding promising performance. However, prompt content and propagation structure are coupled, making it difficult to assess their individual effects and learn compatible configurations. In this paper, we empirically analyze two challenges in learning adaptive policies for topology-based prompting: asymmetric performance effects and coupled configuration selection. We then propose TTPR, a two-stage reinforcement framework that alternately optimizes two policies to generate adaptive configurations, with each policy conditioned on configurations generated by the other fixed policy. These conditional updates separate policy evaluation while preserving configuration compatibility. Specifically, TTPR models an edge-level policy to construct connection patterns and optimizes it with Connection Relative Policy Optimization (CRPO) through group-wise comparisons of complete connection patterns. The other is a node-level policy that generates prompt-node schemes and is optimized with Incremental Node Proximal Policy Optimization (INPPO) through incremental prompt-count decisions and feature generation. Across diverse datasets and pre-training strategies, TTPR ranks first in 8/10 few-shot node classification settings and attains the highest average performance across graph classification benchmarks.

title: Self-Evolving Evaluation Environments for Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are rapidly improving, yet their evaluation remains largely static. Existing benchmarks provide a strong foundation, but fixed difficulty ceilings, limited feature coverage, and coarse aggregate scores progressively weaken their discriminative and diagnostic value. We introduce CUA-SEE, a closed-loop evaluation environment that co-evolves tasks and executable verifiers from rollout evidence. It disentangles three objectives: benchmark evolution expands evaluation scope through cohort-calibrated difficulty and coverage growth; diagnostic evolution increases resolution through agent-conditional capability-boundary probes; and verifier evolution improves precision by translating changing requirements into state-grounded checkpoints with adversarial validation. Across multiple agents, applications, and rounds, CUA-SEE generates challenging, measurable tasks while preserving process-level evidence. Our results position adaptive evaluation as a scalable counterpart to self-evolving agents, continuously tracking what agents can do, where their boundaries lie, and how reliably progress is measured.

title: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference
summary: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,μ\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,μ\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).

title: MedUIGym: Evaluating and Training GUI Agents for Clinical Workflows
summary: Automating clinical workflows requires vision-language agents that can navigate dense graphical user interfaces (GUIs) in electronic health records (EHRs) and execute precise actions, yet many medical agents still rely on text or structured tool calls. In this work, we introduce MedUIGym, a scalable interactive environment comprising 15,739 tasks from 17 benchmark sources across six clinical task families for training and evaluating clinical GUI agents. In MedUIGym, agents perceive EHR states from screenshots and execute mouse-and-keyboard actions, as well as a paired native-tool interface over identical clinical data. The environment verifies both final answers and required clinical actions, and supports parallel trajectory collection for training. Benchmarking twelve vision-language models shows that current agents struggle across diverse clinical workflows, and simply increasing reasoning effort fails to yield consistent gains. Furthermore, MedUIGym supports offline learning from GUI trajectories and online reinforcement learning from task rewards. After training, both Qwen3.5 models perform better on in-domain clinical tasks and generalize to tasks from external sources. By unifying tasks from existing benchmarks, dual-interface evaluation, and GUI trajectory collection, MedUIGym provides a testbed for studying how vision-language agents complete clinical tasks through the EHR's graphical interface. Our project page is available at https://github.com/yitong-qiao/MedUIGym.

title: Tracing Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
summary: Reinforcement learning can increase the success of automated red teaming but it also narrows the attack vector. This study asks where in the attacker-defender-judge learning loop does the narrowing begin and which mechanisms lead to a narrowing attack. Six mechanisms (defender adaptation, success edge, reward reinforcement, row cap, update size, and measurement) are tested across three experiment arms (co-trained, frozen defender, half learning rate) for twenty-four iterations. A frozen defender narrows attack diversity retention (ADR) earlier 0.496 relative to co-trained 0.891 at iteration twelve. Defender updates delay narrowing but dont prevent it. Successful attacks ("winners") have narrower attack diversity than the full set of generated attacks. Attacks closest to previous winners succeed 10-15 percentage points more often than those closest to previous failures. This winner-neighbor advantage holds after a defender update and for a fixed defender too. Attacks with a common opening have a common-opening advantage of 5-16 percentage points. The training row cap and update size account for little impact on ADR, and attack length accounts for only part of the ADR decrease. Narrowing appears to originate from the success only reward through the group-relative training advantage to the attacker update, with a persistent success edge setting the direction.

title: Triage Accuracy of Jev and Open-Weight System One Decision Models and Their Use for Early Emergency Recognition in Symptom-Assessment Applications
summary: Laypeople increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for triage advice, but LLMs answer in variable free text, which makes it hard to evaluate them for use in medical devices. Decision models, which assign a probability to each predefined triage category, may be easier to evaluate. To test their triage accuracy, we evaluated 16 decision models (14 open-weight, 2 proprietary) on 233 synthetic and 10,000 real-world cases, yielding 163,728 total assessments. The best models triaged 72.1% of synthetic cases correctly and agreed with an existing algorithm in 56.1% of real-world cases. They were more promising for recognising emergencies early: given only demographics, chief complaints, risk factors and red-flag answers, the best model reached an AUROC of 0.87. At a 5% error margin, it could decide for or against emergencies for about half of users. Decision models should therefore not replace triage engines but could shorten symptom assessments at setting-specific error margins.

title: Training Dynamics of Large State-Transition Models
summary: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=Ω(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states. Our analysis is based on the bounded trace of the Hessian of the softmax cross-entropy loss, which implies that the approximate second-order stationary points reached by training have high prediction gain. Numerical experiments with practical parameter choices illustrate the persistent training gain and the transfer of the tied model.

title: ComputeWise: Measuring and Fixing GPU Waste by AI Research Agents
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Preliminary version; a revised version is in preparation. Code: https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/computewise. Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/computewise
summary: AI agents are given GPUs to do AI research on their own. Do they use those GPUs well? A busy GPU does not tell us, because it can be busy with work the answer did not need. This matters, because the tokens the agent spends cost almost nothing next to the GPUs its experiments run on, so using those GPUs better has a huge impact. So we built ComputeWise, an open benchmark of research tasks on which this waste can be measured and reduced. For it we developed our own simulated GPU, which replays recorded runs to the agent's code. With no real GPU needed, we ran hundreds of experiments, far more than would be reasonable on real GPUs. With no help, the agents put only 52% of their GPU time into work the answer needed. Another 22% went to work it did not need, and 26% sat idle. Asking the agent to finish the work faster, telling it to keep every GPU busy, or giving it a job scheduler does not fix this. So we built an open-source harness, part prompting and part deterministic code. Across five models, it removed over 80% of the extra time to the answer.

title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
summary: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
summary: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
summary: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.

title: Boltz-Flow: Generating High-Quality Robot Action from Boltzmann Machine
summary: Flow-matching policies integrate a velocity field from a fixed, observation-independent Gaussian source. However, since the source is unimodal and identical across all tasks, the limited representational capacity of Gaussian distributions constrains how far a policy can scale with growing task diversity. Moreover, the source factorizes over time steps and control dimensions, discarding the coordination that manipulation requires. We introduce Boltz-Flow, which replaces Gaussian initialization with a more powerful, observation- and instruction-conditioned Boltzmann source while leaving the base VLA unchanged. Boltz-Flow parameterizes this source with a conditional Boltzmann machine that assigns an energy value to each binary source state. A listwise objective, supervised entirely by offline demonstrations, aligns this energy with the quality of actions produced after frozen flow integration. At inference, the energy defines an Ising instance whose solution is decoded into continuous noise before a single standard integration. We use a physical coherent Ising machine during training. Experiments show that Boltz-Flow improves $π_{0.5}$ across three benchmarks, outperforming the compared strong policy baselines and competing noise optimization methods on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0 and ranking second only to LEAP on LIBERO-Plus. Additional experiments show gains under noise-adapted fine-tuning, with action-to-action warm starts, and on the SmolVLA backbone.

title: PsyDrift: Healthy-Reference Latent Diffusion for Anomaly Scoring in Autism Spectrum Disorder
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at the CVPath-Vision4Neuro Workshop at WACV 2027. Includes expanded related-work and future-work discussion
summary: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $ρ= 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($ρ= -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.

title: Grower-in-the-loop AI for Deployable Precision Fertilisation in Sustainable Agriculture
summary: In agriculture, typically over half of the applied nitrogen fertiliser is lost to water and to air. Precision fertilisation aims to reduce these losses while maintaining yield and quality, yet existing tools struggle to capture farm-specific challenges in determining optimal nitrogen rates. Static recommendations are common and overlook on-farm constraints, such as delays due to weather or machinery availability, or change in budgets. Each constraint governs when and how growers apply fertiliser in practice. Here we present a grower-in-the-loop framework for winter wheat in England, combining baseline fertilisation planning from a machine learning-derived nitrogen-response curve with in-season adaptation via a large language model. We evaluated the framework using data from long-term experiments (LTEs), replicated field trials, and farm deployments. Retrospective model validation using LTEs confirmed low economic decision-loss across multiple seasons. Using field and farm trials, baseline schedules were shown to match standard-practice yields with less nitrogen, whereas in-season adjusted schedules additionally retained grain quality standards. Given this enhanced performance, in-season adaptation absorbed weather, machinery and budget constraints to keep recommendations executable. The framework therefore shows promise for translating static recommendations into adaptable, grower-informed decisions for sustainable fertiliser management.

title: How Latent Transition Geometry Matters for Planning in World Models
summary: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures. This raises a natural question: How does latent transition geometry shape planning? We investigate this through an action-conditioned transition-field view, using curvature regularization as a controlled intervention. Across four continuous-control tasks, appropriately tuned regularization improves planning, while excessive regularization can be detrimental. By decomposing the transition field into affine and non-affine components, we find that regularization reduces action sensitivity mainly through the non-affine component. To assess its role in planning, we directly manipulate the non-affine action response in frozen models and show that it affects candidate selection and closed-loop success. Further analysis shows that curvature generally brings predicted futures closer together, while preserving more of the differences along the goal direction. This helps explain why the planning effects vary across tasks. We observe broadly consistent planning trends across five sampling- and gradient-based solvers on LeWM and similar rollout-geometry trends on DINO-WM. Qualitative attention visualizations reveal accompanying shifts toward task-relevant visual structure. Together, these findings clarify how latent transition geometry influences multi-step planning.

title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.

title: Regularizing Hard Examples Improves Adversarial Robustness
comment: 48 pages, 16 figures, 22 tables. Published in the Journal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR)
summary: Recent studies have validated that pruning hard-to-learn examples from training improves the generalization performance of neural networks (NNs). In this study, we investigate this intriguing phenomenon -- the negative effect of hard examples on generalization -- in adversarial training. Particularly, we theoretically demonstrate that the increase in the difficulty of hard examples in adversarial training is significantly greater than the increase in the difficulty of easy examples. Furthermore, we verify that hard examples are only fitted through memorization of the label in adversarial training. We conduct both theoretical and empirical analyses of this memorization phenomenon, showing that pruning hard examples in adversarial training can enhance the model's robustness. However, the challenge remains in finding the optimal threshold for removing hard examples that degrade robustness performance. Based upon these observations, we propose a new approach, difficulty proportional label smoothing (DPLS), to adaptively mitigate the negative effect of hard examples, thereby improving the adversarial robustness of NNs. Notably, our experimental result indicates that our method can successfully leverage hard examples while circumventing the negative effect.

title: Decoupling Solving from Abstention: Single-Rollout Conformal Risk Control for Hard-Budget LLM Reasoning
summary: Hard token budgets often interrupt LLM reasoning before an answer is produced. Forcing reasoning to terminate recovers correct solutions but also increases confident errors, creating a joint challenge of solving within budget and deciding when to abstain. Existing remedies are costly or lack guarantees: supervised fine-tuning offers no error control, penalizing wrong answers during reinforcement learning (RL) can suppress exploration, and multi-sample conformal methods multiply inference cost. We propose Tail-CRC, a single-rollout framework that separates candidate generation from submission control. We first adapt the solver to budget forcing with pure binary correctness rewards; after freezing it, we apply conformal risk control to upper-tail token surprise in the answer span. Each rollout yields both an answer and an uncertainty score from token log probabilities, enabling finite-sample control of expected wrong submissions under exchangeability and recalibration across risk targets or domains without retraining. We show that wrong-answer penalties create failure-only comparisons in group-relative RL, derive an exploration-starvation boundary, and identify length-induced ranking reversals and single-token spike sensitivity in answer scores. Across Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-8B, 50 RL updates on 400 problems improve correct-submission rates by 15.0--29.6 points on DAPO and 4.3--12.8 points on out-of-domain Omni-MATH over inference-only budget forcing, while reducing generation cost by 3.5--12.6\%. On 8B Omni-MATH, target-domain calibration cuts wrong submissions from 30.3\% to 5.8\% at 4K and from 41.8\% to 6.5\% at 8K. At 4K, generation is 2.05$\times$ faster for 4B and 2.23$\times$ faster for 8B than unforced 8K decoding in local amortized batch time. Tail-CRC thus enables reliable, efficient budgeted reasoning from a single rollout.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy Is Not Deployment Value: Decision-Aligned Reliability Evaluation for Foundation MLIPs in Materials Discovery
comment: 5-page main text plus supplementary appendices; 1 figure, 3 tables in the main text. Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop (AI for Accelerated Materials Design), NeurIPS 2026, Findings & Open Challenges track
summary: In AI-guided materials discovery, machine-learning models increasingly decide which candidate materials should receive expensive first-principles or experimental evaluation. Standard reliability metrics such as uncertainty, calibration, novelty, and ranking accuracy evaluate properties of the predictions, but success on these metrics does not necessarily imply a better downstream screening decision. We study this mismatch for foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MACE-MP, CHGNet, Orb V3) used to rank candidate crystal structures before DFT verification. We evaluate three representative reliability interventions (novelty detection, sparse DFT calibration, and chemistry-level ranking audits) using a deployment objective that measures how much DFT can be avoided while maintaining a required recall of near-hull candidates. Across all three, a reliability signal can succeed on its immediate target without improving the final screening decision: novelty detects distribution shift but weakly ranks failure severity; calibration can improve pooled ranking metrics while leaving screening unchanged or degrading it; and sparse audits identify MLIP-chemistry combinations with poor ranking reliability without yielding a robustly beneficial routing policy. A two-oracle analysis further shows that the source of failure depends on the screening decision itself: under formation-energy screening, even perfect knowledge of average ranking reliability can select the wrong model, whereas in the evaluated hull-aligned variant the oracle target becomes decision-aligned but finite-budget audits still fail to realize the value. Reliability should be evaluated relative to the decision it supports: the relevant question is not whether a model is uncertain or inaccurate, but whether acquiring and acting on additional information will improve the final discovery decision enough to justify its cost.

title: AlphaDefect: Expert-Level AI for Slay the Spire 2
summary: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a single-player deck-building game that requires long-term planning under heavy randomness. We present AlphaDefect, an expert-level AI system for STS2: for each character, one network trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) makes every decision of a run, in combat and outside it. At the highest difficulty, Ascension 10, on two versions of the game current in November 2026 and on test seeds not played in training, AlphaDefect wins 62-77% of runs across six characters with greedy play and 68-80% with test-time search, after 1.3 to 6.7 billion decisions of training per character; runs uploaded by human players of all levels are won 11-20% of the time at the same difficulty. The networks read the game as entity records that identify each card, relic and enemy through a learned embedding and attributes from the game data, together with consequences of public information computed by the engine. Ablations show how much the agent depends on this encoding: without these identities, the network did not win a single run, and without the computed consequences it won 8.3 points fewer. To our knowledge, AlphaDefect is the strongest publicly reported STS2 agent as of November 2026.

title: Stable but Hidden: Identifiability and Experimental Design under Missing Compositional Support
comment: Accepted at the AI for Science Workshop, NeurIPS 2026. 9-page main text plus appendices (53 pages total), 8 figures
summary:
AI-guided scientific discovery often uses inexpensive predictors to allocate scarce verification measurements. We study a structural failure when relevant components have been observed separately but never jointly: distinct admissible response functions can agree on all observed compositions while disagreeing on the missing combinations. Additional same-support data cannot resolve this ambiguity, and agreement among fitted models need not expose it.
  We characterize the unresolved directions as an invisible subspace $\mathcal{N}_T(\mathcal{F}) = \ker \mathcal{R}_T$, whose geometry determines oracle zero-shot ambiguity and minimax risk under a symmetric, bounded ambiguity class. When the missing response lies in an $r$-dimensional, well-conditioned linear basis, optimally designed joint measurements achieve minimax integrated risk $Θ(σ^2 r/m)$, with classical $I$-optimality the fixed-design criterion.
  We validate on materials. In electrocatalysis, a six-dimensional support-derived structural basis (a prior on candidate directions, not an identified physical model) reduces held-out MSE against a dimension-matched generic basis (median paired ratio 0.75, improving 98% of 60 element pairs at $m = 15$), while $I$-optimal and same-basis posterior-variance acquisition show no detected difference. In Materials Project, removing joint property labels reduces $E_{\text{above hull}}$ ranking on 90% of 30 element pairs, more than matched data-removal controls, under a frozen pretrained representation. Pair difficulty is reproducible across learners but poorly predicted by zero-label ensemble disagreement; 20 joint measurements enable transferable pair-level rankings without reliable absolute calibration.
  In practice, experiment selection should ask which relationships the observed support leaves unidentified before asking where a fitted model is least certain.

title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
summary: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.

title: The Growth Path Is the Missing Half of Neural Networks
comment: 27 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Tingan Jin and Haosong Li contributed equally
summary: An artificial neuron computes and learns, but it does not live: the units of a network are fixed when it is designed, and every one of them is kept and paid for whether it is used or not. We give each neuron a second pathway. Beside its Task Path, the usual computation and gradient learning, a dual-pathway neuron has a Growth Path: a nutrient flows from the outputs back through the network, every layer receives the same fixed budget, and each unit is fed in proportion to how much the units above it use it. A well-fed unit divides and a starving unit dies. This allocation is not a separate analysis or pruning step: it runs throughout training and reads only activations and weights. The task is still learned from labels with the ordinary loss, and the training procedure gains no phase, no schedule and no target size. Because the budget is conserved, the competition is zero-sum and a single number sets the size of the network. Switched on in a pretrained network that is deployed on a narrower domain, the Growth Path shrinks the network while it keeps learning. With Adam the network ends 1.0 to 1.2 points more accurate on the domain than the same network trained ordinarily, at 24% to 60% of its compute, and at 12% of the compute it is still ahead; a random choice of the same number of units gives no gain. Letting starving pretrained units sleep instead of die keeps 1.2 to 4.6 points more of the rarely used content. Over 800 changing tasks a network with the Growth Path holds its accuracy while ordinary networks decline. With plain SGD the gains are smaller: at deployment the method trades compute against rarely used content, and on one of the two continual-learning streams it only ties networks of equal size. The experiments are small (three-layer perceptrons on MNIST-like data); what they show is that a conserved, loss-free second pathway can decide by itself which units a network needs.

title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression
summary: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

title: A Polynomial-Time Best-of-Both-Worlds Algorithm for Matroid Semi-Bandit Problems
summary: Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) offers a computationally attractive framework for online learning, with recent advances establishing Best-of-Both-Worlds (BOBW) guarantees for various bandit settings. For matroid semi-bandits, existing methods offering such guarantees primarily rely on Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL), which requires solving an optimization problem at each round. We establish BOBW guarantees for FTPL with Fréchet and Pareto distributions with a certain parameter with geometric resampling in the matroid semi-bandit problem, showing that FTPL can simultaneously achieve the minimax-optimal $O(\sqrt{mdT})$ regret in adversarial setting and a logarithmic regret in stochastic setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm for matroid semi-bandits that achieves BOBW guarantees.

title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
summary: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for selecting subproblems, enabling effective optimization of large-scale CVRP instances. Compared to prior approaches that train task-specific neural networks to select among heuristically constructed subproblems, our method discovers generalizable, interpretable LLM-generated heuristics to directly construct subproblems. Experiments show that our approach achieves comparable in-distribution performance while outperforming neural network-based policies on out-of-distribution instances with large-scale problems.

title: FToken: Factors as Tokens for Dual-Axis Cross-Sectional Return Prediction
summary: On a given trading day, a stock-factor panel describes both how stocks differ across factors and how each factor varies across stocks. Most stock Transformers model relationships among stocks or across time. We introduce FToken, which also models relationships among factors. Its factor branch encodes all stocks' values for one factor as a token, applies self-attention across factors, and maps the result back to one return forecast per stock. A second branch applies attention across stocks in the same panel. A gate combines their forecasts using trailing factor covariance and market volatility. We evaluate both branches on NASDAQ, NYSE, and S&P 500 with the benchmarks' five price features and with 158 factors computed from the same data. On the 158-factor NASDAQ panel, averaging the two forecasts yields an information coefficient (IC) of 0.0421, compared with 0.0392 for the strongest external baseline. The gate raises IC to 0.0443 and gives the highest annualized excess return after costs. The equal-weight ensemble has the higher portfolio information ratio. Both combinations also improve on the strongest external baseline in mean IC on the other two 158-factor panels. On the five-feature NYSE panel, the differences are within the variation across seeds. ```

title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
summary: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. As AI also makes decisions about work allocation, we compare a set of LLMs. We find many models also deviate from purely objective decisions, particularly when the project stakes are low, but there is wide heterogeneity as to how much and in what manner they weigh enjoyment. These results raise questions about what role human experience may play in decisions around where and how to integrate AI into workplaces. Integration may be jagged across settings due to consideration not only of the relative capabilities of workers, but also the human experience of work, the valence of that experience (e.g., more strongly weighing aversion), the context (e.g., stakes), and who is making or guiding such choices (human or LLM).

title: Grokking as a Subspace Search: Computing the Destination Before Training
summary: Grokking is the phenomenon in which a neural network generalizes long after it has memorized its training data. Many explanations have been proposed for the delay between memorization and generalization. However, none of them can say before training where the network is heading, so they cannot be tested against one another. We show that on group tasks this destination can be computed from the task itself before training begins. It is a low-dimensional subspace of the network's embeddings, which we call the right subspace, and we prove that it is essentially unique. Knowing the destination makes our hypothesis falsifiable: the delay is a search for the right subspace, and generalization begins when the network finds it. When we give the network the right subspace from the start, the delay disappears. When we take the right subspace away, accuracy stops at a ceiling that we compute before training, and on multiplication the network cannot generalize at all. When we train the network normally, its embeddings move toward the right subspace by themselves, long before test accuracy rises. Finally, interventions during training show that this search sets the length of the delay, and that noise in the optimization does not. On every group task that we tested, grokking is a search for the right subspace, and the delay is the time that this search takes.

title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop PTA: From Pretrained Representations to Acting Agents
summary: Speaking early turns a prediction into an irreversible public commitment. We introduce SayWhen, a test-time controller that selects a task-directed act shared across typed continuation plans and controls its release as speech. A persistent veto blocks playback when intervening transcripts invalidate the candidate. We define regret-free early speech (RFES) to measure supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility. On a 72-prefix branching diagnostic, the generated-plan frontier attains 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret, versus 8.2% RFES and 0.068 regret for Matched Top-One. Measured planner latency constrains this path; a deterministic retail schema attains 31.7% RFES, compared with 32.0% for the complete policy. In a separate 30-task $τ$-Voice simulation, schema-derived candidates with cached text-to-speech (TTS) audio attain 21/30 task-level RFES. Eligible audio begins 1.51 seconds before the user-audio endpoint among the 22 tasks with early speech, or 1.11 seconds over all 30 tasks with zero for tasks without eligible early speech. Semantic veto and endpoint waiting each pass 16/30 tasks. Together, the studies demonstrate a controlled coverage-compatibility trade-off and schema-based pre-endpoint operation, making the supported public commitment an explicit unit of voice-agent control.

title: LambdaLens: Auditing a Representation-Changing Hyperparameter in Graph Neighbor Embedding
summary: Changing a graph embedding parameter can change what the layout represents. In SG-t-SNE-$Π$, the rescaling parameter $λ$ changes the probability assigned to each neighbor before optimization begins. We introduce LambdaLens to trace that change from individual edges to the resulting layout. For nodes with at least two neighbors, we derive a normalized power path. When the original weights are unequal, the number of neighbors determines where the weights become uniform and where their ordering reverses. Near $λ=1$, the rate of change in each edge probability depends on its surprisal relative to the neighborhood entropy. To measure the geometric effect, we vary $λ$ while holding the input graph, initialization, random seed, and optimizer settings fixed. Across six graphs, some layouts continue to move as $λ$ increases, others stabilize early, and others barely move. PubMed has the widest relative spread in node degree, yet its layout changes little. On four datasets with class labels, four probes recover 98.48-100% of the best label-fidelity score on a 16-value grid, using 75% fewer evaluations. In a six-dataset comparison, SG-t-SNE-$Π$ attains the highest observed primary score on four datasets and ranks among the top three on all six. On Citeseer, four probes come close to the dense-grid optimum, yet PHATE better preserves class structure, making a change of embedding pipeline worth considering on that graph. ```

title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop AgenticOS: Co-designing Systems and ML Foundations of an OS Layer for Agentic AI
summary: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.

title: STMemoLLM: A Spatial-Temporal Memory-Augmented LLM for Robust Traffic Forecasting
summary: Traffic forecasting is essential for intelligent transportation systems. However, traditional deep-learning models often rely heavily on high-quality observations. Recent LLM-based approaches incorporate pretrained knowledge to improve forecasting, but they remain sensitive to input perturbations and struggle to preserve long-term patterns. To address this, we propose STMemoLLM, a spatial-temporal memory-augmented LLM for robust traffic forecasting. STMemoLLM introduces memory prototypes to compress inputs into compact summary tokens while extracting reliable dynamics from residual signals, achieving a balance between stability and variability. Specifically, a memory-enhanced tokenizer encodes prototypes and sensor characteristics into attention biases to guide adaptive compression of correlated sensors into semantic summary tokens. A memory-calibrated router further evaluates contextual deviation, compression deficiency, and prototype alignment to identify reliable residual signals, which complement the summaries while suppressing noise. Extensive experiments on eight real-world datasets show that STMemoLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional experiments examine point masking, additive Gaussian noise, structured missingness, and limited training data, demonstrating strong robustness. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/STMemoLLM-70BF.

title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

title: Revisiting Continual Learning in Language Models: A Three-Interface Diagnosis of Stability and Plasticity
summary: Continual learning in language models is commonly studied in the incremental learning (IL) setting, where a model learns a sequence of tasks and is evaluated through its final classifier or language-model (LM) head. This interface, however, does not indicate where forgetting occurs: a drop in accuracy may reflect representation degradation in the backbone, readout mismatch in the head, or both. We therefore argue that backward transfer (BWT) and forward transfer (FWT) should be interpreted as interface-dependent quantities rather than as single modellevel properties. We study three evaluation interfaces: the trained head, which is updated sequentially with the backbone; a probe newly trained on frozen backbone features; and a classifier-free backbone diagnostic. They measure deployed performance, recoverability under a new readout, and representation separability, respectively. Across class-incremental experiments with encoder and decoder language backbones, plus task-incremental sanity checks, conclusions about forgetting and plasticity change with the interface: the trained head often indicates severe forgetting, the probe near-complete recoverability, and the backbone diagnostic intermediate representation drift with a consistent negative relation between stability and plasticity. This relation holds for clustering-free diagnostics such as nearest-class-mean accuracy and across five clustering algorithms and three metrics. Finally, Just LM-Head Tuning (JLT), a head-only intervention on a fixed incrementally trained backbone, recovers 96-99% of the gap to joint training for replayand distillation-based methods but only about three quarters for plain sequential fine-tuning, suggesting that many failures attributed to catastrophic forgetting reflect head-backbone mismatch plus partial representation drift. Our results call for reporting where forgetting is measured, not only how much.

title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
summary: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

title: IADR: Interface-Augmented Neural Operator for Phase-Field Mean-Curvature Flow
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 34 pages, 5 figures. Qinyi Zhang and Duanyu Feng contributed equally. Yangshuai Wang and Hao Wang are co-corresponding authors. Code: https://github.com/ArcueidCroft/IADR
summary: The Allen-Cahn equation is one of the standard phase-field models for mean-curvature flow (MCF), parameterised by the diffuse-interface width $\varepsilon$. Practical simulations span a range of $\varepsilon$, so a single model covering this range is needed. PDE-specific neural operators are accurate but must be retrained at every $\varepsilon$; general neural operators cover $\varepsilon$ in one model but lose the phase-field structure of the target. We introduce Interface-Augmented Diffusion-Reaction (IADR), a neural operator that addresses both shortcomings: a target network with a diffusion-and-reaction (DR) structure preserves the phase-field structure of the Allen-Cahn equation, while a hypernetwork that maps $\varepsilon$ to the weights of this target network amortises the dependence on $\varepsilon$ across the range. A single IADR matches the per-$\varepsilon$ specialists on in-distribution data within the prescribed range, retains their cross-shape generalisation under both $\varepsilon$- and geometry-out-of-distribution shifts, and retains their compact DR target structure with millisecond-scale inference. We further establish a conditional $K$-step rollout error bound under consistency and stability assumptions.

title: Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences
summary: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate's genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment-contig-isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall.

title: AdaptRouter: Adaptive Routing across Evolving Tasks and Models
summary: Model routing assigns each query to a suitable foundation model, but tasks and available models keep changing, and existing routers are either untrained for the pool at hand or fit once and forget earlier tasks when updated. We present AdaptRouter, an adaptive router trained by policy learning: a compact multimodal decision model reads each question with cards describing the current experts and learns from native task feedback, without routing labels, to select one frozen expert. Open-weight and API experts share the router, its inputs, and the quality-cost trade-off but use different losses: cheap open-weight experts are explored with RL, whereas paid API experts are queried once and their cached feedback is reused as soft labels. New tasks are learned without replay, new experts enter as cards, and an open-weight quality-first advantage provably keeps cost from overriding quality. Across four task stages, AdaptRouter loses at most 0.4 points on earlier tasks, whereas feedback-trained routers lose up to 7.0, and as its pool grows from three to ten experts, its accuracy rises from 67.2% to 72.1%. On five API models, it exceeds GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra (low) by over 22 points at under a third of their cost.

title: Habitats: A Framework for Open-Ended Evolution of Agent Objectives
comment: To be published in the Managing Agents that Manage Agents Workshop on Responsible Use of Meta-Agents at the Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (2026)
summary: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every population reward, producing a cross-fitness matrix that exposes self-mastery, transfer, and functional diversity. A population-level Planner uses this information to select parent rewards and issue targeted mutation directives, while a separate Mutator translates those directives into validated reward programs. We evaluate Habitats in a discrete Card Sandbox and three continuous-control environments (Cart-Pole, Hopper, and Cheetah) against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines. Across four environments and three random seeds, Habitats achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity, with final diversity reaching 1.8x that of Direct Mutation and 2.5x that of Independent Generation. Finally, across ten downstream objectives unseen during evolution, frozen Habitats policy libraries achieve higher paired win rates than size-matched Direct Mutation and Independent Generation libraries at 10,000 adaptation episodes, while also surpassing task-specific policies trained from scratch for 20,000 episodes. These results suggest that separating population-level planning from reward synthesis enables the discovery of diverse, learnable, and reusable behaviors.

title: PackLoop: Row-Packed Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models under Concurrency
summary: Looped language models reuse one block of weights T times per token, trading parameters for test-time depth, but autoregressive decoding then pays T sequential passes per token. Self-speculative decoders recover 2-10x for a single request, yet their gains fade as requests share a GPU, and current practice is to speculate less as load grows. We show that what fails under load is the layout of speculative work, not speculation. In concurrent decoding the unit of cost is the row, one request advancing on one loop, which reads that loop's key-value (KV) cache once; additional positions inside a row are nearly free. Pipelined schedules such as the wavefront place every speculative position on a different loop, hence in a row of its own, so each token is still read T times. We present PackLoop, built on one principle: speculate only inside rows that are read anyway. Deep loops accumulate positions and advance them as a block in one row, context-copy proposals join the row that the first loop already reads, and a closed-form admission rule, the economic order quantity of inventory theory, sets how long to accumulate from a cost model calibrated once per engine. PackLoop is exact: in FP32 its output is token-for-token identical to autoregressive decoding, also under sampling and early exit. Across 164 load points spanning three GPUs, four Ouro models, six benchmarks, and contexts up to 32K tokens, one PackLoop configuration is faster than the best existing schedule, chosen per point, at 161 points (median 1.25x, up to 1.76x) and never significantly slower. Its lead grows with concurrency and context length, the regime in which existing self-speculation gains least.

title: When Does Overriding the Majority Vote Help?
summary: When should additional reasoning or verification replace a majority-vote answer? We call such a replacement an override. We examine two obstacles: the availability of correct alternatives and the reliability of methods that produce or select them. We compare additional reasoning, executed programs, and cross-model reasoning on 150 competition-mathematics questions with three open reasoning models. Starting from a majority vote over 16 responses, we measure how often overrides occur and how many errors they correct or introduce across agreement thresholds. When the vote is incorrect, the correct answer is often absent from the original responses. Additional same-model reasoning rarely overrides, while executed programs correct more errors than they introduce at every evaluated threshold. Cross-model overrides improve some weaker baselines but do not establish an advantage over the more accurate model alone, even with only eight standalone responses. Stricter agreement reduces how often overrides occur but does not consistently increase the fraction that correct errors. At the strictest thresholds, overrides occur on few distinct questions, limiting conclusions about their reliability.

title: Composing Independently Distilled Memory and Retrieval Policies for Long-Term Agents
summary: Long-lived Web assistants require effective memory and retrieval mechanisms to access information from past user interactions. While these capabilities can be learned through specialized policies, it remains unclear whether specialists trained independently in different environments can be effectively composed without joint optimization. This paper investigates compositional transfer through policy distillation. Memory-writing and sequential retrieval policies are independently distilled from frontier-model action trajectories into 3B models and combined with a fixed answer generator without downstream training. On a LongMemEval-based benchmark, the distilled composition achieves 73.1% accuracy, compared with 36.2% for a composition of existing RL-trained specialists, and also outperforms the evaluated RL-trained compositions on PersonaMem-v2. Component ablations reveal that improvements in individual policies depend on their composition, highlighting the importance of cross-specialist compatibility. Further task-specific adaptation improves accuracy to 75.2% on LongMemEval through RL and 48.9% on PersonaMem-v2 through supervised distillation. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of independent specialist distillation for modular multi-agent systems. Source code and datasets of teacher-generated memory-editing and retrieval trajectories are released to facilitate reproducibility and further research.

title: Reducing Order Sensitivity in Decision Models
summary: Decision models are emerging as fast components of larger AI systems. Yet recent decision models, such as Jev, process options sequentially, leading to different predictions based on their ordering. Across ten open- and closed-source decision models, we find that \emph{order-sensitivity} is pervasive, causing substantial accuracy degradation and unreliable decision-making. These effects become more pronounced as the number of options grows and can compound across multi-step decisions. To address this problem, we systematically compare eight methods for mitigating order sensitivity in terms of robustness, predictive accuracy, and inference efficiency. Among these methods, we find that \emph{tree attention} is a surprisingly effective and efficient method. It achieves order invariance by processing options as parallel branches of a shared context. When used during training, it matches the baseline's average accuracy. Applied to the baseline without retraining, it also eliminates order sensitivity with only a 1.1-point drop in accuracy. Our findings demonstrate that order invariance can be enforced directly in decision models with little or no loss in predictive accuracy.

title: Operator-Valued Q-Learning: Compositional Bellman Recursions for Order-Sensitive Decision Making
summary: In quantum pulse sequences, spacecraft attitude control and in-hand reorientation, actions act on a hidden physical state as non-commuting operators, so the outcome of a plan depends on the order of its actions. We let the value function carry this structure: each Q(s,a) is an N x N operator, and the Bellman backup applies the action's dual map to the continuation value, Q(s,a) = K_a^*(R(s,a) + gamma E V(s')). Unrolled along a plan, the recursion builds the ordered product of the actions' operators, and the value at any latent state is a linear trace readout. It is exact for policies that do not observe the latent, the backup contracts for unitary and orthogonal dynamics, and an asynchronous operator TD scheme learns it with almost-sure convergence. Classical values live in a lattice, so a maximum over actions exists; self-adjoint operators form an anti-lattice (Kadison) and have none. An operator log-sum-exp still gives one operator per state-action pair whose readout upper-bounds the value of every policy at every latent state. The sampled update converges to it for a finite horizon, and it reduces to soft Q-learning and the QMDP bound when actions commute. We prove that scalar values on observations that ignore action order must confuse swapped histories, that exact history tables grow exponentially for free action groups but polynomially for nilpotent ones, and give a Hankel-rank lower bound on the operator dimension. In experiments the learned policy matches 1000-simulation tree search on SO(3) pointing for horizons up to 20 at ~10^4 times lower decision cost, transfers zero-shot to unseen initial states, and acts exactly on its belief mean when the initial state is hidden, where plugging the mean into a DQN does not. A planner with the same model knowledge is more sample-efficient at short horizons, and a DQN given the operators matches or exceeds OpQ.

title: Needwise: Generation-Free Conversational Recommendation from Need-Level Typed Decisions
summary: Conversational recommenders must rank items against needs that catalogs record only in part, while users add, withdraw and reverse needs and switch between requests. LLM rankers re-read the dialogue at every turn: they are slow, and their ordering does not show which needs an item meets. We show that a conversational recommender can be built from typed decisions instead: named questions over fixed options, answered with option probabilities rather than generated text. On each turn, one typed request maps the message onto the catalog's fields, keeps what no field expresses in the user's words, and decides how the turn changes each earlier need. Needwise then ranks candidates must-first: the needs on the kind of item, its place and its price form a tier, and within it one holistic decision and need-level verdicts (supported, contradicted or unknown) are combined with equal weight (Needwise-HF).
